lessons.title: A cross-section is not a population: prevalence, incidence and who is missing from the snapshot
lessons.explanation:
Every clinical encounter produces a cross-section: one person, one day, one set of findings. Almost every number a clinician reads about mental disorder is also a cross-section, but of a population rather than a person, and the two kinds of snapshot fail in the same way. They report what is present at a moment and say nothing about how it got there or how long it will stay. This lesson supplies the arithmetic that connects the snapshot to the process underneath it, and it is the foundation for the rest of this level, because prognosis, relapse and service planning are all statements about time.

Three quantities have to be kept apart. Incidence is the number of new cases arising in a defined population over a defined period, conventionally per 100,000 person-years. Prevalence is the proportion of that population with the condition at a point (point prevalence) or at any time in a window (period prevalence). Duration is how long a case remains a case. At steady state, and for a condition whose incidence is not changing rapidly, prevalence is approximately incidence multiplied by mean duration. The relation is an approximation, and it is the most useful approximation in this lesson: it converts two numbers that are usually reported separately into a test of each other. A pooled incidence of psychotic disorders of 26.6 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 22.0 to 31.7) across 177 studies implies that a prevalence of roughly 0.4 per cent corresponds to an average duration in the region of fifteen years, which is what a disorder with sustained disability and incomplete recovery would produce. If the two figures implied a duration of six months, one of them would be measuring something else.

The consequence for clinical samples is structural. A prevalent pool accumulates people in proportion to how long they stay in it, so long-duration cases are over-represented and brief cases are almost absent. Neyman's original observation about hospital samples is the general form: selecting on presence at a moment selects on duration, and if duration is related to severity, exposure or outcome, the sample is biased in a direction that is not random. A community team whose caseload is 34 per cent psychotic disorder is not evidence of an epidemic; it is evidence that the team's door and the disorder's duration together produce that mix.

The second filter is ascertainment. Incidence estimates differ by method as well as by place: in the same meta-analysis, population registers reported higher rates of non-affective psychosis than first-contact study designs, with a rate ratio of 9.64 (2.72 to 31.82) for non-affective disorders, which is far too large to be a difference in morbidity and is a difference in who gets counted. Heterogeneity across studies was extreme (I squared at or above 98.5 per cent), which means a pooled figure is a summary of very different measurements rather than a description of a uniform world. Men had higher rates of all psychotic disorders (incidence rate ratio 1.44, 1.27 to 1.62) and ethnic minorities higher rates still (1.75, 1.53 to 2.00); those are the kinds of contrast that survive such heterogeneity better than the absolute level, because they are comparisons made within studies.

What follows for reading a paper. First, identify the denominator: which population, defined how, counted when. Second, identify the numerator: what case definition, applied by whom, with what ascertainment. Third, ask which quantity is being reported and whether the claim being made requires a different one: a service planning claim needs prevalence and duration, a prevention claim needs incidence, and a claim about unmet need needs both plus the treatment gap. Fourth, treat any figure drawn from a clinical sample as a statement about that sample until a population-based estimate is produced. The WHO World Mental Health Report's summary figures, about one in eight people living with a mental disorder and 71 per cent of people with psychosis not in contact with services, are population statements, and they are the right comparison for a clinic's composition.
lessons.example:
A fictional early intervention team is asked to justify its expansion. It offers three numbers: 210 people on its caseload, 34 per cent of whom have a psychotic disorder; a local survey finding of 0.6 per cent prevalence of psychotic disorder; and a published incidence of 27 per 100,000 person-years. The board asks whether the team is over-subscribed.

Work through the arithmetic. If incidence is 27 per 100,000 per year in a catchment of 400,000, about 108 new cases arise each year. If average duration in contact is eight years, prevalence in contact is roughly 0.2 per cent, or about 864 people, of whom the team sees 210, around a quarter. The local survey's 0.6 per cent is a broader definition and includes people not in contact, which is consistent. Nothing here suggests an epidemic; the numbers suggest partial coverage of a long-duration condition, which is a different and more useful finding.

Now the caseload mix. Thirty-four per cent of 210 is about 71 people with a psychotic disorder. If the team also holds 60 people with bipolar disorder, 40 with severe personality disorder and 39 with other long-term difficulties, the caseload is dominated by conditions with long durations and high relapse rates, which is exactly what a secondary care team should look like. The same team would look very different if it were a primary care sample or a crisis line.

The board's question, whether the team is over-subscribed, is not answerable from these numbers at all, because it requires a standard of coverage per head of population and a statement of what the team is expected to do. What the arithmetic does supply is the size of the population the team is responsible for, and the observation that its caseload represents roughly a quarter of prevalent cases in contact with any service. That is the kind of statement a board can act on, and it could not have been produced by reading the caseload alone.
lessons.question: A fictional paper reports that 41 per cent of attendees at a specialist mood clinic meet criteria for bipolar disorder, and concludes that bipolar disorder is under-recognised in the community because community prevalence is only about 1 per cent. What is the central error?
lessons.answer: The clinic proportion is a property of a prevalent, referred sample, not of the population: it is produced by referral selection and by duration, and it cannot be compared with a community prevalence estimate to support a claim about under-recognition.
lessons.distractor: The error is the use of a 1 per cent prevalence figure, since contemporary community surveys find substantially higher rates and the comparison would be sound with a corrected denominator.
lessons.correction: The denominator error survives any correction to the prevalence figure, because the two numbers describe different populations selected in different ways. A mood clinic is a place people are sent when a mood problem is suspected and retained when it persists, so both filters favour bipolar disorder over brief or untreated conditions. The claim about under-recognition may be true, but this evidence cannot support it: it would require a population-based estimate of unmet need, or a comparison of detection rates against a structured assessment in a defined sample. The transferable move is to ask, of any proportion, what the denominator is and how people got into it, which is the question this lesson exists to install.

depth.definitions:
Incidence: new cases per population per unit time, usually per 100,000 person-years. Point prevalence: the proportion with the condition at one moment. Period prevalence: the proportion affected at any time in a window. Mean duration: average time a case remains a case, including treated and untreated time. Steady state: the condition in which incidence and prevalence are not changing, so prevalence approximates incidence times duration. Length bias (Neyman bias): the over-representation of long-duration cases in samples selected on presence at a point in time. Ascertainment: the process by which cases become known to a study, which determines whether they are counted. Denominator: the population in which a count is expressed. Treatment gap: the proportion with a condition who are not receiving care.

Prerequisite: lesson 31 on levels of description and lesson 50 on reading a study. Nothing here is a method for assessing a person.
depth.mechanism:
Why does prevalence behave like incidence times duration? Imagine a population in steady state where 100 new cases arise each year and each remains a case for five years on average. In any year, the pool contains the cases that arose in each of the last five years, roughly 500 people, so prevalence is five times the annual incidence. The pool is a queue: inflow is incidence, outflow is recovery, death and migration, and the size of the queue is inflow multiplied by waiting time.

Two consequences follow immediately. The first is compositional: the pool is weighted toward slow exits, so if duration depends on severity, the pool over-represents severity even when incidence is unrelated to it. The second is that a change in either term changes prevalence, so a rising prevalence figure can reflect better survival, longer treatment, earlier detection or genuine increase in onset, and the arithmetic alone cannot distinguish them.

Ascertainment is the second mechanism. A case exists for a study only if it passes through the case-finding procedure: a register, a first-contact service, a survey interview. The same underlying morbidity produces different counts through different procedures, which is why the meta-analytic variation in psychosis incidence was so extreme and why register-based rates exceeded first-contact rates by a large factor. That is not measurement error in the ordinary sense; it is a difference in the definition of the numerator.

Finally, the arithmetic is a check, not a proof. It assumes steady state, which mental disorders often violate: onset is concentrated in youth, cohorts differ, and services change. Its proper use is to detect inconsistency, not to establish truth.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting case, chosen because it reverses the direction of the bias. A fictional memory clinic reports that 62 per cent of its attendees have a dementia syndrome, and a commissioning group uses this to argue that dementia is the dominant mental health problem of older age. Here the clinic is a tertiary referral service with a diagnostic function, so its composition reflects the referral question rather than prevalence: general practitioners refer when they suspect cognitive decline, and the clinic's purpose is to confirm or exclude it. The pool is selected on the suspicion, not on the disorder's duration.

Compare with a community survey of the same age band reporting 6 per cent prevalence of dementia and 12 per cent of clinically significant anxiety. The survey's denominator is the population and its ascertainment is systematic, so its proportions can be compared with other populations; the clinic's cannot. Both numbers are true and they answer different questions: the clinic's answer is about the yield of a referral pathway, which is useful for planning clinic capacity, and the survey's is about the distribution of need, which is useful for planning services.

The instructive part is that neither sample is biased in a way that makes it useless. The clinic's 62 per cent is exactly what a well-functioning diagnostic service should show, and a clinic showing 6 per cent would be doing something else. The error is never that a selected sample exists; it is that its proportion is exported into a sentence about the population. Reading a paper well means noticing when that export has happened, and the tell is usually a comparison between a clinical proportion and a community prevalence in the same paragraph.
depth.mistake:
The commonest error is the denominator swap: quoting a proportion from a clinic, a trial or a case series as though it described a population. It is attractive because clinical proportions are vivid and easy to obtain, and because the person quoting them often has no population estimate to hand. The diagnostic question is simple: who could have been in this sample and was not?

The second error is treating a pooled incidence or prevalence as a single world fact. The psychosis meta-analysis found heterogeneity at or above 98.5 per cent, which means the pooled estimate summarises a distribution so wide that the average describes almost no setting. When heterogeneity is that large, the useful output is the pattern of contrast (by sex, by ethnicity, by ascertainment method) and the range, not the point estimate.

The third error is reading a rise in prevalence as a rise in incidence. Because prevalence is inflow times duration, improved survival, earlier detection and longer treatment all raise it without any change in how often the condition begins. A service that reduces mortality among people with severe mental illness will, other things equal, increase measured prevalence, which is a success that looks like a failure when the two quantities are confused.

The fourth error belongs to service planning: using caseload counts as a needs assessment. Caseload is a function of the referral pathway and the team's capacity, not of population need, and a team that is hard to refer to will have a small caseload and unmet need around it.

Diagnostic routine: for any figure, write down numerator, denominator, time window and ascertainment method. If any of the four is missing, the figure is not yet usable.
depth.application:
Take a paper that reports both a prevalence and an incidence for the same condition, and do three things in writing, in no more than 250 words.

First, compute the implied mean duration by dividing prevalence by incidence, taking care with units (convert prevalence to a proportion, incidence to a proportion per year, then divide). State the result in years and say whether it is plausible for the condition, given what you know about its treated course.

Second, list the ascertainment differences between the prevalence and incidence estimates: were they from the same study, the same population, the same case definition, the same period? If not, say which of the two figures you would trust for a service planning claim and why.

Third, take one clinical sample from the same paper, or from a related paper, and state explicitly what its composition cannot tell you. A single sentence of the form 'this proportion describes who was referred and retained, not how common the condition is' is sufficient if it is specific about the two filters.

A worked miniature, so the shape is clear. Suppose prevalence 0.35 per cent and incidence 25 per 100,000 per year. Then 0.0035 divided by 0.00025 per year gives 14 years. That is plausible for a disorder with sustained disability, and it means a team holding 300 such patients is holding roughly one year's incident cohort plus thirteen years of accumulated cases, which is a useful way to think about what a caseload actually is.
depth.summary: Prevalence is approximately incidence times duration, so the two numbers check each other and a clinic's composition tells you about duration and referral rather than about how common a condition is. Samples selected on presence at a moment over-represent long cases, and ascertainment method can change measured incidence by an order of magnitude. Heterogeneity at the level reported in the psychosis literature means a pooled figure describes a distribution, not a place. The practical habit is to name numerator, denominator, time window and ascertainment before using any frequency figure, and to treat clinical proportions as statements about the pathway that produced them.

readings.title: Jongsma, H. E., Turner, C., Kirkbride, J. B. and Jones, P. B. (2019), 'International incidence of psychotic disorders, 2002-17: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Lancet Public Health 4(5):e229-e244
readings.note: Read the findings section for the pooled incidence of 26.6 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 22.0 to 31.7), the heterogeneity figures (I squared at or above 98.5 per cent), the sex and ethnicity rate ratios, and the meta-regression result that population registers reported far higher rates than first-contact designs. That last result is the cleanest demonstration in the literature that measured incidence depends on ascertainment. The discussion is candid about the limits of pooling widely varying studies.

readings.title: Kessler, R. C. et al. (2005), 'Lifetime prevalence and age-of-onset distributions of DSM-IV disorders in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication', Archives of General Psychiatry 62(6):593-602
readings.note: Read the abstract for the survey method and the headline estimates (any disorder 46.4 per cent lifetime; anxiety 28.8 per cent; mood 20.8 per cent; median age of onset 11 for anxiety, 30 for mood). Use it as a model of how a population prevalence is actually produced: a structured interview, a household sample, a defined recall window. The full text is paywalled; the abstract carries the numbers used in this lesson.

readings.title: World Health Organization (2022), 'World mental health report: transforming mental health for all'
readings.note: Read Chapter 1 for the population-level prevalence and treatment-gap figures (about one in eight people living with a mental disorder; 71 per cent of people with psychosis not in contact with services) and Chapter 3 for how those estimates are constructed. These are the population statements against which any clinic's composition should be compared. Note that the report is a synthesis for advocacy and planning, not a primary analysis, and its figures inherit the uncertainties of the surveys behind them.

visual.title: Incident flow into a prevalent pool, with the filters that shape a clinic caseload
visual.description: A flow diagram showing how new cases enter a population pool, how long they stay, and how referral and retention produce the composition a clinic sees.
steps: Left: incidence box, labelled with a rate per 100,000 person-years and its case definition and ascertainment method (register, first contact, survey). State that changing ascertainment changes the inflow without changing the underlying morbidity.

Centre: the prevalent pool, drawn as a wide queue, with mean duration annotated and the identity prevalence approximately equals incidence times duration written beside it. Mark that the pool over-represents cases with long duration.
Exits from the pool: recovery, death, migration out of area, and disengagement. Note that exits are the reason a prevalence figure can rise when mortality falls, without any change in incidence.

Right, upper branch: referral filter into secondary care, labelled with the referral question (who is sent, by whom, with what threshold). Right, lower branch: retention filter, labelled with what keeps people in contact (severity, relapse, legal status, unmet social need).

Far right: the clinic caseload box, with a note that its composition reflects both filters and cannot be compared with a population prevalence. Add the diagnostic question: who could have been in this sample and was not.
Bottom band: three quantities to state before using any figure, numerator, denominator, time window, plus ascertainment method as a fourth.

lessons.title: Prognosis is a probability, not a property: base rates, discrimination and calibration
lessons.explanation:
Lesson 46 established that predicting who will die by suicide is limited by the rarity of the outcome and by the weakness of the available predictors, and that a risk assessment is a structured conversation rather than a forecast. This lesson can assume that and add the technical vocabulary that makes the limit precise. The vocabulary matters because clinicians are now routinely shown numbers produced by models: a flag in an electronic record, a score in a discharge summary, a percentage from a risk calculator. Reading those numbers requires three separate judgements that are often collapsed into one.

The first is discrimination: how well the model ranks people. The usual summary is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, the probability that a randomly chosen person with the outcome scores higher than a randomly chosen person without it. An area of 0.5 is chance, 0.7 is modest, 0.8 is good for many outcomes and rare in psychiatry. Discrimination is a property of ordering and says nothing about the level of risk.

The second is calibration: whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. A model can rank perfectly and still be badly calibrated; if it gives everyone twice their true risk, the ordering is intact and every number is wrong. Calibration is assessed by plotting observed against predicted risk across groups, by the calibration slope (ideally 1, with values below 1 indicating overfitting and above 1 indicating underfitting) and by the calibration-in-the-large. The calibration literature is blunt about why this matters: a model that is miscalibrated cannot be used for decisions that depend on absolute risk, however good its discrimination, and calibration is the property most often omitted from reports.

The third is clinical utility: whether using the model at a particular threshold does more good than harm. A decision curve compares the net benefit of acting on the model against acting on everyone and against acting on no one, across a range of threshold probabilities. Utility is not implied by either of the first two properties, because it depends on what the decision costs.

Then there is the arithmetic that no model escapes. Positive predictive value depends on prevalence. At a base rate of 2 per cent, an instrument with sensitivity 0.70 and specificity 0.75 produces a positive predictive value around 5 per cent: most flags are false. The same instrument at a base rate of 20 per cent produces a positive predictive value near 40 per cent. The model has not changed; the population has. This is why a risk tool validated in a secondary care sample can perform unimpressively in primary care, and why transporting a threshold across settings is a substantive error rather than a technicality.

The evidence on suicide prediction is the clearest case. A meta-analysis of 365 studies and 3,428 risk factor effect sizes covering fifty years found that prediction of suicidal thoughts and behaviours was only slightly better than chance across odds ratio, hazard ratio and diagnostic accuracy analyses, that no category of risk factor performed far above chance, and that predictive ability had not improved over five decades. Studies rarely tested combinations of factors, and the homogeneity of the literature meant the meta-analysis could not approximate most theories. The authors' conclusion was that the field needed to move from single risk factors to multivariable, machine learning based algorithms, a recommendation that is itself a hypothesis rather than a demonstration.

The clinical implication is not that prediction is worthless but that its products have a specific shape. A model with modest discrimination and good calibration can support a conversation about probability and can direct a scarce intervention to a group with elevated risk. It cannot tell a clinician which individual will deteriorate, and it cannot convert a base rate of 2 per cent into a plan for one person. Risk assessment retains value as a structured way of ensuring that known modifiable factors are addressed, which is a different function from forecasting.
lessons.example:
A fictional trust introduces a machine learning flag for post-discharge self-harm, developed on three years of local data. The reported area under the curve is 0.68. The outcome occurs in about 3 per cent of discharges within 90 days. A ward manager is told that 200 patients per year will be flagged as high risk and asks how many of them will actually self-harm.

Do the arithmetic. Of 1,000 discharges, 30 have the outcome. If the model's sensitivity at the chosen threshold is 0.60, 18 of those are flagged. If specificity is 0.80, then 20 per cent of the 970 without the outcome, 194 people, are also flagged. Total flags: 212. Positive predictive value: 18 divided by 212, about 8.5 per cent. So of the 200 flagged patients, roughly 17 will have the outcome and 183 will not.

Now vary the threshold. Raising it so that specificity reaches 0.95 flags 48 people and captures, say, 8 of the 30 cases: positive predictive value rises to about 17 per cent, but 22 of the 30 cases are missed. Lowering it captures more cases and dilutes the flag further. This trade is not a defect of the model; it is the structure of testing for a rare event, and it is why the choice of threshold is a policy decision about which error the service prefers.

What the manager can do with the number. She can staff an intervention for 200 people, knowing that most will not have the outcome, and she can justify that if the intervention is low burden and moderately effective. She cannot tell a patient that he is high risk and expect that statement to be accurate; the honest form is that his estimated risk is several times the average, that most people in his position do not self-harm, and that the plan is about what would help if things deteriorated. That is what a well-calibrated probability is for: it shapes the plan and the monitoring, not a verdict.

Finally, she should ask about calibration explicitly. If the development sample was drawn from a different service with a different discharge policy, the predicted probabilities may be systematically wrong even if the ranking holds, which is exactly the situation in which a flag should be recalibrated locally before it is used in conversations with patients.
lessons.question: A fictional paper reports a new prognostic model for transition to psychosis with an area under the curve of 0.78 in an independent sample, and states that it 'identifies individuals who will develop psychosis with 78 per cent accuracy'. The authors recommend using it to select people for a preventive intervention. What is the main technical error in that sentence?
lessons.answer: The area under the curve is a discrimination statistic, not a percentage of correct individual predictions; a value of 0.78 says the model ranks cases above non-cases with that probability, and the proportion of flagged people who develop psychosis still depends on the base rate and on the threshold chosen.
lessons.distractor: The error is the use of an independent sample, since predictive models must be validated in the population where they were developed before any performance statistic is meaningful.
lessons.correction: Independent validation is the strength of the study, not its flaw; the error is the interpretation of the statistic. Discriminative accuracy of 0.78 means that if you pick one person who transitions and one who does not, the model orders them correctly about 78 per cent of the time. In a sample where 10 per cent transition, a threshold capturing most cases will also flag many who do not, and positive predictive value may sit near 30 per cent. The recommendation to select people for preventive intervention therefore requires two further analyses the sentence does not report: calibration in the target population, and a decision analysis at the threshold the service would actually use. Note also that the intervention's own harms and the availability of effective prevention determine whether even a well-calibrated 30 per cent risk justifies selection, which is a question for the decision curve rather than for the model.

depth.definitions:
Prognosis: the expected course of a condition in a defined group, expressed as a probability over a stated time horizon. Prognostic model: a combination of predictors producing an individual probability. Predictive model (treatment-effect): a model identifying who responds differently to a treatment, a distinct object from a prognostic one. Discrimination: the ability to rank cases above non-cases, summarised by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Calibration: agreement between predicted and observed risk, assessed by calibration plot, calibration slope and calibration-in-the-large. Brier score: an overall measure combining discrimination and calibration. Net benefit: the value of a decision rule at a threshold, accounting for false positives and false negatives. Positive predictive value: the proportion of those flagged who have the outcome, which depends on prevalence. Transportability: whether performance holds in a population other than the development one.

Prerequisite: lesson 46 on risk assessment, and lesson 76 on heterogeneity and individual prediction. This lesson is about reasoning with probabilities; it is not a method for assessing a person's risk.
depth.mechanism:
Why does prevalence dominate predictive value? Because a test applied to a population with few cases mostly encounters non-cases, and even a modest false-positive rate applied to a large number of non-cases generates many flags. The algebra is unforgiving: positive predictive value equals sensitivity times prevalence, divided by that quantity plus (1 minus specificity) times (1 minus prevalence). As prevalence approaches zero, the second term in the denominator dominates whatever the sensitivity, so predictive value collapses toward zero. No modelling sophistication changes this, because it is a property of the arithmetic rather than of the algorithm.

Why are discrimination and calibration separable? Discrimination depends on the spread of predicted risks relative to the spread of true risks; calibration depends on their level. Multiplying every predicted risk by two preserves ordering and destroys calibration. Overfitting in development produces predictions that are too extreme: the model has learned noise, so high predicted risks are too high and low ones too low, which shows as a calibration slope below 1. Shrinkage and penalisation address this, and external validation tests whether it worked.

Why does clinical utility need a separate analysis? Because the cost of a false positive and a false negative are not equal and vary by decision. The decision curve converts the model into net benefit at a threshold probability, where the threshold encodes the ratio at which a clinician would accept a false positive to gain a true positive. A model can be the best available and still have negative net benefit at the threshold a service would use, which is the finding that should stop an implementation rather than the size of the area under the curve.

Finally, why does the suicide prediction literature look so bleak? Partly because the outcome is rare and the predictors are weak, and partly because the studies were homogeneous in design. The meta-analysis could only assess narrow associations, and its own authors noted that the literature had not tested the combinations that theories of suicide require. A field that has measured the same categories for fifty years will produce a flat result whether or not prediction is possible in principle.
depth.secondExample:
A contrast in the same service, chosen because the outcome is common. A fictional community team builds a model to predict unplanned admission within 12 months after a crisis episode. The outcome occurs in 22 per cent of episodes, the model's area under the curve is 0.66, and its calibration slope is 0.95 with predictions tracking observed risk closely across deciles.

Apply the same arithmetic. With 220 events per 1,000 episodes, sensitivity 0.55 and specificity 0.75, the flag captures 121 events and 195 false positives, giving a positive predictive value of 38 per cent. The discrimination is no better than the self-harm model's 0.68, and the flag is far more informative, because the outcome is a fifth of the population rather than a fiftieth.

This pair is the lesson. Two models, similar ranking ability, radically different clinical usefulness, and the difference is the base rate. A clinician shown both numbers without the prevalence would rank them in the wrong order. A service deciding where to deploy a limited care coordinator would be right to choose the admission model, because a 38 per cent hit rate supports a caseload of 200 with 76 true positives, and a 8.5 per cent hit rate supports a caseload of 200 with 17.

Now the second half of the reading, which concerns what happens after the model is deployed. Suppose the team uses the admission flag to allocate care coordination, and admissions fall. The model's predictors included previous admissions, so the intervention changes the very variable the model uses: the model degrades because the service improved, which is a general problem with deploying prognostic models as interventions. The team should expect to recalibrate, and should treat the model as a moving estimate rather than a fixed instrument. That is the difference between a prognostic claim and a property of a person.
depth.mistake:
The first error is reading discrimination as accuracy. An area under the curve of 0.78 does not mean 78 per cent of predictions are correct; it is a rank probability, and the proportion correct depends on the threshold and the base rate. This mistake is endemic in press coverage and in grant applications, and it survives because the statistic sounds like a percentage.

The second error is treating a risk category as a prediction. Calling someone high risk after using a tool that has been shown to have poor predictive value is not a neutral act: it changes observation, restricts liberty, and can be recorded as a finding. NICE guidance on self-harm advises against using risk scales and tools to predict repetition, and it does so because the evidence does not support the prediction, not because assessment is unnecessary.

The third error is assuming that adding predictors to a rare outcome will fix predictive value. Adding variables improves discrimination slowly and marginally; it does not change the base rate, which is the dominant term. Enthusiasm for machine learning in suicide prevention rests partly on this misunderstanding, and the honest position is that better models may improve triage at the margin while remaining unable to identify individuals.

The fourth error is transporting a threshold. A cut-off chosen to yield a manageable number of flags in one service will yield a different number and a different predictive value in another, because both prevalence and case mix differ. Thresholds are local decisions requiring local validation.

The fifth is the inverse error, dismissing models altogether because prediction is imperfect. A model that modestly improves the concentration of a scarce resource can be worth using, provided its calibration is checked and its outputs are framed as probabilities rather than verdicts.

Diagnostic routine: for any model, obtain discrimination, calibration and the base rate, then compute what a flag means in the population where it will be used.
depth.application:
Take one published prognostic or risk model in mental health and produce a one-page appraisal with four sections.

Section one, the claim and the population: what outcome, over what time horizon, in what population, and with what intended decision. Note whether the model was developed and validated in the same sample.

Section two, performance: report discrimination with its confidence interval, calibration as reported (plot, slope, or in the large), and the base rate of the outcome in the validation sample. If calibration is not reported, write that down as a gap rather than assuming it is adequate.

Section three, the arithmetic: choose the threshold the paper recommends, take its sensitivity and specificity, and compute positive predictive value at the reported prevalence. Then recompute at half and at double that prevalence, to see how the flag behaves in a different service. Show the two by two table explicitly.

Section four, the decision: state what a clinician could and could not say to a patient given these numbers, and what additional evidence would be needed before the model was used to allocate a resource.

A worked miniature. If a paper reports sensitivity 0.62, specificity 0.88 and a 4 per cent base rate, then per 1,000 people: 40 cases, 25 flagged, and 115 false positives from 960 non-cases, giving a positive predictive value of about 18 per cent. Doubling prevalence to 8 per cent gives 50 true flags from 80 cases and 110 false positives, a positive predictive value near 31 per cent. The same test, two populations, two very different conversations.
depth.summary: Discrimination, calibration and clinical utility are separate properties, and a model can be good at one and useless for the decision at hand. Predictive value is governed by prevalence, so the same instrument behaves very differently in a clinic and in a community, and a threshold is a local decision. Fifty years of suicide prediction research has produced discrimination only slightly better than chance, which is why guidance advises against risk categorisation tools. The usable product of a model is a calibrated probability supporting a plan, never a statement about which individual will deteriorate.

readings.title: Franklin, J. C. et al. (2017), 'Risk factors for suicidal thoughts and behaviors: A meta-analysis of 50 years of research', Psychological Bulletin 143(2):187-232
readings.note: Read the abstract in full for the design (365 studies, 3,428 effect sizes) and the findings: prediction only slightly better than chance across odds ratio, hazard ratio and diagnostic accuracy analyses; no improvement across fifty years; five broad categories accounting for nearly 80 per cent of risk factor tests. Note the authors' own recommendation of machine learning approaches; it is presented as a hypothesis about method, not as a demonstration that such models work. The full text is paywalled and the abstract carries the key figures.

readings.note: Open access. Read the sections defining calibration, the distinction between calibration-in-the-large and calibration slope, and the argument that discrimination without calibration cannot support decisions based on absolute risk. Read also the worked examples of miscalibration that look acceptable on a summary statistic. This is the technical basis for the second of the three judgements in this lesson; skip the more mathematical passages on the first reading.

readings.title: NICE (2022), 'Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence', NICE guideline NG225
readings.note: Read the recommendations on assessment of risk, in particular the advice against using risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, together with the recommendations on what assessment should cover instead (needs, circumstances, safety planning). The contrast between the two halves is the practical version of this lesson: prediction is discouraged, structured assessment of modifiable factors is required. The guideline pages are the authoritative version; quotes should be taken from the live page rather than from secondary summaries.

visual.title: From model output to a sentence a clinician can say
visual.description: A four-stage decision flow that separates discrimination, calibration, predictive value and clinical utility, with the question asked at each stage.
steps: Stage 1, discrimination: does the model rank cases above non-cases? Report the area under the curve with its confidence interval and ask whether the validation was external. Warning marker: any statement that the value is a percentage of correct predictions.

Stage 2, calibration: do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies? Look for a calibration plot or slope. Warning marker: no calibration reported, or calibration assessed only in the development sample.

Stage 3, base rate and predictive value: write the two by two table at the intended threshold and the prevalence of the setting where the model will be used. Compute positive predictive value. Warning marker: a threshold imported from another service.

Stage 4, utility: would acting on the flag at this threshold do more good than acting on everyone or on no one? Name the intervention, its burden, and the cost of a false positive. Warning marker: a recommendation to use the model with no statement of what happens after a flag.

Terminal box, the sentence: what the clinician may say (an estimated probability relative to the average, with the time horizon), what they may not say (that this person will or will not deteriorate), and what the plan does with the information.

lessons.title: Relapse, recurrence and the arithmetic of maintenance
lessons.explanation:
Maintenance treatment is the part of psychiatry where the arithmetic of risk is most often misstated, and where the consequences of misstatement are largest, because the decision is made with a person who is currently well. Lesson 83 supplies four things: a vocabulary that separates the phases of illness, the arithmetic that converts trial results into quantities a person can use, the design features that make discontinuation trials easier to misread than to read, and the limits of what a trial can say about the individual in front of you. Nothing here is dosing guidance, and decisions about starting, continuing or stopping treatment belong to the person and their clinician.

The vocabulary first. Response is a measurable improvement, conventionally a halving of symptom severity. Remission is a threshold state, often defined as being below a cut-off for a defined period. Recovery adds a duration and a functional criterion, usually several months to years of remission. Relapse is the return of the index episode after response or remission but before recovery; recurrence is a new episode after recovery. The boundaries are conventions, and different trials draw them differently, which is the first thing to check when comparing relapse rates across studies: a trial with a lenient relapse definition will report more relapse.

The arithmetic. Absolute risk reduction is the difference between event rates; the number needed to treat is its reciprocal, and it is meaningless without a time frame. The meta-analysis of antipsychotic maintenance in schizophrenia, 65 trials and 6,493 patients, found relapse at one year in 27 per cent of people continuing antipsychotic and 64 per cent of those randomised to placebo, a risk ratio of 0.40 (0.33 to 0.49) and a number needed to treat of 3 (2 to 3). Readmission was 10 per cent against 26 per cent, a number needed to treat of 5. The same trials reported harms: weight gain 10 per cent against 6 per cent, movement disorders 16 per cent against 9 per cent, sedation 13 per cent against 9 per cent. Note that fewer than a third of people who relapsed were admitted, which is why readmission is a weaker outcome than relapse and why a service that counts only admissions will understate the burden.

Design features change what the numbers mean. Most maintenance trials use a randomised discontinuation or withdrawal design: everyone is stabilised on treatment, then a subset is randomised to continue or to stop, often with placebo substitution. Three consequences follow. First, the sample is enriched for people who tolerated and responded to the drug, so the absolute risks apply to that group rather than to everyone who starts treatment. Second, abrupt withdrawal can produce symptoms that resemble relapse, and unblinding through side effects allows both participants and assessors to infer allocation, which inflates the difference. Third, the trial's time horizon sets the question: a twelve month relapse rate says nothing about five years.

There is a mirror-image design problem in the psychological literature. Trials of relapse prevention therapy often compare an active course against treatment as usual after acute response, and the comparator may be minimal, so the estimated effect includes attention, structure and expectancy as well as the specific technique. The question a clinician actually faces is comparative: continuing what, compared with what, for how long, for this person.

What individual factors modify the average. The strongest consistent modifiers are the number of previous episodes, the presence of residual symptoms at the point of remission, and the abruptness of discontinuation. A person with three prior episodes and residual symptoms is at higher risk than the trial average, and a person tapering slowly after a first episode with full remission is at lower risk. The trial supplies a baseline; the person supplies the modifier; the decision is theirs.

The honest formulation of the whole matter is that maintenance treatment trades a reduction in the probability of relapse against the burdens of continuing: side effects, monitoring, cost, the meaning of being a person who takes medication, and the difficulty of stopping later. Those burdens are not soft considerations to be weighed after the numbers; they are the other side of the ratio, and they differ between people with identical relapse risks.
lessons.example:
A fictional 24-year-old man has had a first episode of psychosis, responded well over four months, and now asks whether he can stop his antipsychotic. He has no residual symptoms, has returned to work, and finds the weight gain and sedation difficult. His clinician has the meta-analysis to hand.

Work the numbers into a form he can use. Over one year, continuing treatment is associated with relapse in about 27 per cent and stopping with about 64 per cent, so for every three people who continue for a year, one relapse is avoided. His personal estimate is likely better than the trial average for continuation and worse for stopping, because he has had only one episode but is early in recovery, which is the period of highest risk. The harms also apply to him: weight gain and sedation are the two he is already experiencing, and the trial rates for movement disorders and sedation are averages across drugs and doses.

Present the decision as three questions rather than one. What would he be trading? A reduction of roughly 37 percentage points in one-year relapse risk, against continued side effects and monitoring. What would stopping look like if he chose it? A planned taper with monitoring, a written plan for early signs, and agreement about what would trigger a review, since abrupt cessation is itself a risk factor. What would change the recommendation? A second episode, residual symptoms, a deterioration in sleep or functioning, or a family history of severe illness would all move the estimate upward.

Then the part that is not arithmetic. He may value avoiding a second episode very highly, or he may value being off medication very highly, and those valuations are not in the trial. The clinician's job is to make the trade explicit and to keep the plan revisable, which means the decision is recorded as provisional with the conditions under which it would be reviewed. That is what a good maintenance conversation looks like: numbers on the table, burdens named, plan written down, review dated.
lessons.question: A fictional guideline panel writes that because continuing antipsychotic treatment reduces relapse by 60 per cent, services should prioritise maintenance for all patients, and that the number needed to treat of 3 shows the benefit is large. What is the most important correction to this sentence?
lessons.answer: The number needed to treat of 3 is specific to one year and to the stabilised, tolerant trial population, the 60 per cent is a relative reduction, and the same trials show harms that a service-level recommendation must carry: the sentence has converted a time-bound estimate in a selected group into an unrestricted policy.
lessons.distractor: The number needed to treat of 3 is arithmetically implausible for a relapse outcome and indicates that the meta-analysis pooled heterogeneous trials, so neither figure should be quoted.
lessons.correction: The number needed to treat is correct for what it measures: with 27 per cent against 64 per cent at one year, the absolute difference is 37 percentage points and its reciprocal is about 2.7, rounded to 3. The errors are scope errors rather than arithmetic ones. The trial population had already stabilised and tolerated treatment, so it excludes the people who stopped early because of side effects, who are precisely the people for whom a policy of universal maintenance is hardest to implement. The time frame is one year, and relapse risk is not constant over years. The relative figure travels badly and the absolute figure travels only with its time frame and population attached. A defensible panel statement would give the pair of risks, the time frame, the harms, and the subgroups in which the balance differs.

depth.definitions:
Response: a defined improvement, commonly a 50 per cent reduction in symptom severity. Remission: a threshold state sustained for a stated period. Recovery: sustained remission with functional restoration, usually over months or years. Relapse: return of the index episode before recovery. Recurrence: a new episode after recovery. Absolute risk reduction: the arithmetic difference between event rates in two groups. Number needed to treat: the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction, always attached to a time frame and an outcome. Randomised discontinuation design: stabilise everyone, then randomise to continue or withdraw. Enrichment: selecting participants on prior response or tolerance, which raises observed response rates. Withdrawal (discontinuation) phenomena: symptoms following reduction or cessation that can mimic relapse. Censoring: the handling of participants whose outcome is not observed for the full period.

Prerequisite: lesson 76 on average effects and heterogeneity, and lesson 29 on shared decisions. This lesson is not dosing guidance and does not replace a clinical discussion.
depth.mechanism:
Why does a discontinuation trial tend to overstate the benefit of continuing? Start with who enters. Participants must have responded and tolerated treatment during an open stabilisation phase, so the sample is a survivor cohort: people who had intolerable side effects or did not respond have already left, and they are the people for whom the real-world decision is hardest. Their exclusion raises the observed continuation benefit in the trial relative to a clinic.

Then consider what withdrawal does. Many psychotropic drugs produce discontinuation symptoms on abrupt cessation, and some of those symptoms overlap with the symptoms being measured, so an assessor scoring a withdrawal syndrome may record a relapse. Blinding is imperfect because side effects are detectable, and participants who notice they are no longer taking an active drug may report differently. Both mechanisms push the same way.

Then consider time. Relapse risk is highest early after cessation, so a trial with a short follow-up captures the steepest part of the curve and reports the largest difference. A trial with five-year follow-up would report a smaller average annual difference and a larger cumulative one, and neither number is wrong; they answer different questions.

Finally, consider the comparator in psychological relapse prevention trials. If the control is treatment as usual with minimal contact, the contrast includes the non-specific components of therapy, which lesson 78 described. The specific technique's contribution can only be isolated against an attention-matched control, and few trials provide one.

The arithmetic of the number needed to treat has its own mechanism. Because it is a reciprocal, it behaves non-linearly: a change from 64 to 27 per cent gives a number needed to treat of 3, while a change from 20 to 15 per cent gives 20. Two interventions with the same relative reduction can differ tenfold in the number of people who must be treated, which is why relative statements cannot be ranked against each other and absolute ones can.
depth.secondExample:
A different condition and a different design, to show that the reasoning transfers. A fictional woman of 52 has had three episodes of major depression, the most recent eighteen months ago, and has remained well on an antidepressant at the dose that achieved remission. She asks about stopping because she dislikes the idea of long-term medication and has read that withdrawal can be severe.

The evidence has a different shape here. Maintenance trials in recurrent depression typically show a substantial reduction in relapse over one to two years for continuing treatment against withdrawal, with absolute differences in the region of 20 to 30 percentage points, so the number needed to treat is again in the low single figures for that period. Her prior episode count places her above the average risk, and her sustained remission without residual symptoms places her below it. The two modifiers pull in opposite directions, which is the ordinary situation and the reason an individual estimate is a judgement rather than a calculation.

The design features matter for what she has read. Discontinuation symptoms are common and can be prolonged, and a trial that stops treatment abruptly will attribute some of what follows to relapse; a guideline that recommends tapering is responding to that overlap. Equally, a trial in which everyone was stabilised for months before randomisation tells her about people like her, not about people who never reached remission.

The useful clinical move is the same as in the first example: name the trade, put the absolute numbers on the table with their time frame, describe what stopping would involve if she chose it (a slow taper, a written early warning plan, a review date), and state what would change the estimate. The decision is hers, and the plan is revisable: that is not a concession to uncertainty but the correct form of a decision made under it.
depth.mistake:
The commonest error is quoting a relative reduction as though it were the benefit to the person. 'Sixty per cent less likely to relapse' is true in the trial and is heard as 'sixty per cent protection', and the difference between those readings is the difference between the two event rates. The correction is mechanical: always convert to the pair of risks plus the number needed to treat plus the time frame.

The second error is treating the number needed to treat as a fixed property of a drug. It is a property of the comparison, the population, the outcome and the duration, and it changes when any of those change. A number needed to treat of 3 for relapse at one year in stabilised patients is not a number needed to treat of 3 for hospital admission over five years in a first-episode clinic.

The third error is reading relapse as evidence that treatment failed. A person who relapses after stopping may have relapsed because the treatment was doing something, which is the inference the trial supports, or because withdrawal produced symptoms that were treated as relapse, which is a different event with a different implication.

The fourth error runs the other way: treating a demonstrable maintenance benefit as an obligation. The trial establishes an average advantage, not a duty, and the burdens fall on the person who takes the drug. A formulation that presents continuation as the only rational choice has stopped being a formulation and become a directive.

The fifth is forgetting the denominator. Maintenance trials enrol people who reached remission and stayed in the trial; clinic populations include many who never did. Applying trial relapse rates to everyone who has ever had the diagnosis overstates both the risk and the benefit.

Diagnostic routine: write the two rates, the difference, the reciprocal, the time frame, and the population the rates came from, in that order, before speaking.
depth.application:
Take one maintenance or relapse-prevention trial and produce a two-column conversion sheet.

Left column, the trial as reported: the outcome and its definition, the two event rates, the risk ratio with confidence interval, the follow-up duration, the population and how it was selected (open-label run-in? prior response required?), and the harms reported with their rates.

Right column, the conversion: absolute risk reduction as a percentage, number needed to treat with its time frame, number needed to harm for each important adverse event, and one sentence stating what the trial can and cannot say about a person who does not resemble its participants.

Then write the shared decision paragraph in no more than 80 words, containing the two risks with the time frame, the number needed to treat, the main burden, and the review condition. A worked model: 'Over one year, about 27 in 100 people who continue treatment relapse, compared with about 64 in 100 who stop, so continuing prevents one relapse for every three people treated. The costs are the side effects you are already noticing, mainly weight and sedation. If you choose to stop, we would taper slowly and meet at six weeks and three months, and if sleep or functioning changed we would review the plan.'

Finally, mark which parts of that paragraph came from the trial and which came from the person's circumstances. The distinction is the whole skill: the trial supplies the rates, and the person supplies the modifiers, the values and the decision.
depth.summary: Response, remission, recovery, relapse and recurrence are conventions, and comparing rates across trials requires checking how each was defined. Absolute risks, their difference and the number needed to treat, always with a time frame, are the usable form of maintenance evidence; the antipsychotic meta-analysis gives 27 per cent against 64 per cent at one year, a number needed to treat of 3, alongside measurable harms. Discontinuation designs enrich for tolerant responders and confound withdrawal with relapse, so their estimates describe a selected group over a short horizon. The decision belongs to the person, and the plan it produces should be recorded as revisable.

readings.title: Leucht, S. et al. (2012), 'Antipsychotic drugs versus placebo for relapse prevention in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Lancet 379(9831):2063-2071
readings.note: Read the abstract for the primary figures used in this lesson: 65 trials, 6,493 patients, relapse at one year 27 per cent on drug against 64 per cent on placebo, risk ratio 0.40 (0.33 to 0.49), number needed to treat 3; readmission 10 per cent against 26 per cent, number needed to treat 5; and the harms (weight gain, movement disorders, sedation). Note that fewer than a third of those who relapsed were admitted, which is why readmission is the weaker outcome. Full text is paywalled; the abstract carries the numbers.

readings.title: NICE (2022), 'Depression in adults: treatment and management', NICE guideline NG222
readings.note: Read the recommendations on maintenance treatment (continuing treatment beyond the acute episode for people at risk of relapse, and for how long) and the recommendations on stopping treatment, including tapering and the recognition of withdrawal symptoms. The two sections together are the practical form of this lesson's argument: continuation is offered on the basis of relapse risk, and stopping is a planned process rather than a default. Use the live guideline rather than summaries, since recommendation wording is revised.

readings.title: Henssler, J. et al. (2022), 'Description of antidepressant withdrawal symptoms in clinical practice guidelines on depression: a systematic review', Journal of Affective Disorders 316:1-10
readings.note: Read the abstract for the finding that guidelines vary substantially in how they describe withdrawal and how far they distinguish it from relapse. This is the source for the design problem in this lesson: if withdrawal symptoms overlap with the symptoms being counted, a discontinuation trial can record a withdrawal syndrome as a relapse. Read critically: a review of guideline text is a review of documents, not of incidence, and it cannot tell you how often withdrawal occurs.

visual.title: The maintenance decision as four quantities and one conversation
visual.description: A decision flow that converts a relapse-prevention trial into a shared decision, with the population and time frame carried at every step.
steps: Box 1, the trial: two event rates over a stated period (for example 27 per cent continuing against 64 per cent withdrawn at one year), with a note on who was eligible and whether an open-label stabilisation phase preceded randomisation.
Box 2, the conversion: absolute difference (37 percentage points), number needed to treat (3), number needed to harm for each important adverse event, and the time frame written next to every number.

Box 3, the modifiers: prior episode count, residual symptoms, abruptness of any taper, concurrent psychosocial support. Arrow labelled 'moves the individual estimate up or down', with the direction of each modifier shown.

Box 4, the trade: benefit on one side, burdens on the other (side effects, monitoring, cost, identity, difficulty stopping later), drawn as a balance rather than a sum, because the weights are the person's.
Box 5, the plan: what will be taken or not, the taper if stopping, the early warning signs, the review dates, and the conditions under which the plan would be revised. Mark the whole box 'revisable'.
Footer: a line separating what the trial supplied (rates) from what the person supplied (modifiers, values, decision), because collapsing the two is the error this diagram exists to prevent.

lessons.title: Dose, duration and the shape of response: what titration trials can and cannot show
lessons.explanation:
Lesson 56 described medication classes conceptually and noted that effects lag; this lesson takes the two variables that clinicians actually adjust, dose and time, and asks what the trial literature establishes about each. The answer is less intuitive than the practice. Neither variable behaves the way a linear model would predict, and the reasons are informative about how drugs act and how trials are built.

Start with dose. The default assumption, that more drug produces more effect, is a hypothesis with a testable shape. In fixed-dose trials the shape is usually a plateau, and in many cases the best balance between efficacy and tolerability sits at the lower end of the licensed range rather than at the top. A systematic review of flexible titration, drawing on 123 placebo-controlled trials and 29,420 participants, compared trials that allowed upward titration above the minimum licensed dose with those using the fixed minimum dose. For SSRIs the ratio of odds ratios for response was 0.96 (0.73 to 1.25), which is to say no evidence of additional benefit, and there was no important difference in tolerability or acceptability. For mirtazapine the estimate was 0.77 (0.33 to 1.78). The exception was venlafaxine, where titration from 75 to 150 mg gave a ratio of 1.30 (1.02 to 1.65).

That result is worth understanding rather than memorising. Three mechanisms produce a plateau. The first is receptor occupancy: for SSRIs, the therapeutic effect is mediated through transporter blockade that is substantially complete at modest doses, so higher doses add adverse effects more reliably than they add efficacy. The second is dropout: in a trial, participants who experience side effects stop, and a dose that causes more side effects lowers the average outcome by removing people from the analysed group, which can make a higher dose look no better than a lower one even if it is more potent. The third is heterogeneity of response: a subgroup may benefit from higher doses, and an average across everyone will not detect it.

Now duration. The claim that antidepressants take four to six weeks to work is partly a statement about measurement and partly about averaging. Early improvement, assessed at two weeks, predicts later response reasonably well and predicts non-response better: the absence of any early change is a moderately useful signal that the current strategy is unlikely to succeed, which is the basis for measurement-based decisions to adjust. But prediction at the individual level is modest, as lesson 82 would lead you to expect, and many people who improve late would have been switched unnecessarily if early non-improvement were treated as failure. The practical implication is to measure early and often, and to treat the trajectory rather than a single cut-off.

The sequenced treatment literature complicates this further. STAR*D followed outpatients through up to four acute steps with measurement-based care: remission rates by self-report were 36.8 per cent at step one, 30.6 per cent at step two, 13.7 per cent at step three and 13.0 per cent at step four, with a cumulative remission rate of 67 per cent, and those requiring more steps had higher relapse rates in follow-up. The figures are widely quoted and they describe what happened in an open-label trial without a placebo arm, with substantial attrition between steps, and with treatment choices partly determined by patient preference. They establish that many people need more than one attempt and that later attempts succeed less often; they do not establish the comparative value of any particular sequence, because there was no randomisation to sequences at the level of the overall strategy.

A cleaner comparison of settings is instructive. When the same measurement-based protocol was delivered in primary and specialty care, remission rates were nearly identical (26.6 per cent against 28.0 per cent by clinician rating; 32.5 against 33.1 by self-report), supporting the conclusion that identical care produces identical outcomes across settings. That finding belongs to lesson 86's argument about delivery, and it also undercuts the assumption that intensity of setting is itself therapeutic.
lessons.example:
A fictional patient has been on an SSRI at the minimum licensed dose for six weeks. Her score has fallen from 19 to 13 on a scale where remission is below 5. She has had no side effects and asks whether she should double the dose.

Work through what the evidence supports. Six weeks at an adequate dose with a partial response is a common situation, and the options are usually described as continuing, increasing, switching or augmenting. The titration literature directly addresses the increase option: across 123 trials, flexible upward titration above the minimum licensed dose did not produce a detectable average benefit for SSRIs (ratio of odds ratios 0.96, 0.73 to 1.25), and did not worsen tolerability in aggregate. That is an average, and the confidence interval includes both a 27 per cent reduction and a 25 per cent increase in the odds of response, so the honest statement is that the average effect is close to zero and the individual effect is uncertain.

What else should enter the conversation. First, whether the six weeks included an adequate dose from the start, since a common cause of apparent non-response is a subtherapeutic exposure for part of the period. Second, the trajectory: a fall from 19 to 13 is real improvement, and the question is whether it is continuing. Third, residual symptoms and functional state, since a person who is back at work with mild symptoms is in a different position from one who is not. Fourth, her preferences and her tolerance of the alternatives, which include switching to a drug with a different mechanism and adding a psychological treatment.

How the decision would be recorded. Rather than 'increase dose', the note should say what is being tested: a further four weeks at the current dose to see whether the trajectory continues, or an increase with a review at four weeks against a stated target, and what would happen if the target were not met. The trial evidence says the increase is unlikely to be harmful on average and unlikely to be a large gain on average; the plan converts that into an experiment with a review date, which is what a partial response deserves.

One caution belongs here. Nothing in this lesson is dosing guidance; the numbers describe average trial behaviour, and the decision requires the prescriber's knowledge of the drug, the person's history and interactions.
lessons.question: A fictional service protocol states that the minimum licensed dose should be used first, doubled at four weeks if response is incomplete, and doubled again at eight weeks, because 'the dose-response curve is steepest at the top'. A trainee objects that the evidence does not support this. Which statement best characterises the disagreement?
lessons.answer: The protocol assumes a monotonic dose-response that the trial literature does not show for SSRIs, where flexible titration above the minimum licensed dose has not added efficacy on average, and it imposes a fixed schedule in place of a measured trajectory; the evidence would support continuing at the minimum dose with monitoring, or a deliberate trial of an increase with a review, but not a routine doubling ladder.
lessons.distractor: The trainee is wrong because higher doses are more effective in fixed-dose trials, and the only issue with the protocol is that it does not specify a symptom measure.
lessons.correction: The protocol's premise is the error: for SSRIs and mirtazapine, the ratio of odds ratios for flexible titration above the minimum licensed dose was 0.96 (0.73 to 1.25) and 0.77 (0.33 to 1.78), with no important tolerability difference, and the fixed-dose literature places the best efficacy and tolerability balance in the lower part of the licensed range. Venlafaxine is the documented exception, where titration from 75 to 150 mg added benefit. A second problem is that a doubling ladder substitutes a rule for a measurement: the same four-week review of a measured trajectory, with a stated target and an alternative if the target is missed, is what the evidence can inform. Protocols do real work in services, but a protocol that encodes an untested assumption becomes a citation for it.

depth.definitions:
Dose-response curve: the relation between dose and effect, which may rise, plateau or fall depending on the outcome and the drug. Fixed-dose trial: participants are randomised to set doses, which allows the shape of the curve to be estimated. Flexible titration: dose adjusted upwards within a protocol according to response and tolerability, which tests a strategy rather than a dose. Ratio of odds ratios: the comparison of treatment effect between two sets of trials, here titrated against fixed-dose. Early improvement: change in symptom score within the first two weeks, used as a predictor of later response. Adequate trial: a threshold of dose and duration conventionally used to judge whether a treatment has had a fair chance, not a guarantee of response. Sequenced treatment: successive treatments offered after an inadequate response. Remission: a defined threshold state, usually below a cut-off score for a stated period.

Prerequisite: lesson 56 on medication classes and lesson 73 on measurement and meaningful change. This lesson describes average trial behaviour and is not prescribing guidance.
depth.mechanism:
Why would a higher dose not produce more effect? Because the target is usually near-saturated. SSRI efficacy is mediated by serotonin transporter occupancy, and typical therapeutic doses occupy a large majority of transporters; beyond that point the marginal pharmacological effect is small while the marginal adverse effect is not. Occupancy studies and fixed-dose trials agree on the shape, which is why the plateau is a pharmacological finding and not an artefact of trial design.

Why would a higher dose sometimes look worse? Because of what happens to the denominator. In an intention-to-treat analysis, participants who drop out for adverse effects contribute their last observation or are counted as non-responders. A higher dose increases dropout for adverse effects, so the analysed group at the higher dose contains fewer people who stayed long enough to respond. This is a real effect on the outcome being measured, not a statistical nuisance, and it is why tolerability and efficacy cannot be evaluated separately when the outcome is a mean score in a trial population.

Why does the flexible titration design test a strategy rather than a dose? Because the comparison is between two policies: start low and go up as needed, versus stay at the minimum. The policy bundles a dose range with a decision rule and a timing, and its result is a statement about the policy. A clinician who follows the policy with one patient is applying a policy result to a person, which is the same inferential step as any other average, with the same requirement to check whether the person resembles the trial population.

Why is duration not a fixed latency? Because response is distributed. Some people improve in the first week, most of the improvement that will occur happens by four to six weeks in responders, and a minority improve later. A threshold of four weeks therefore classifies some eventual responders as non-responders, and the cost of that misclassification is a switch that was not needed. Measurement of trajectory, rather than a single assessment at a conventional time, is the response to a distribution that has no sharp edge.
depth.secondExample:
A different decision at the same point, chosen because it shows what the sequence literature can and cannot support. A fictional patient has not responded to two adequate trials of different SSRIs and asks whether a third switch or an augmentation is more likely to work.

What the evidence offers is a set of step remission rates from an open-label sequence: about 37 per cent at step one, 31 at step two, 14 at step three, 13 at step four, with a cumulative 67 per cent. Read as a curve, later steps have lower success. Read causally, the curve cannot compare strategies, because the people entering later steps differ from those who remitted earlier (they are more treatment-resistant by definition), and because the choice of strategy at each step was not randomised at the level of the overall plan.

So the honest answer to the patient separates three questions. What is the chance that the next step works at all? Around one in seven in that cohort, which is low but not negligible, and higher in a clinic that has not yet tried the specific options. Which next step? The sequence data cannot rank them; comparisons of switching against augmenting require randomised trials, and the differences found in such trials are usually modest, with the choice often turning on side-effect profiles and the patient's preference. What happens if this step fails? The cumulative figure already includes people who needed four steps, and the follow-up data show higher relapse among those who required more steps, which is information about prognosis rather than about the next drug.

The transferable method is to state the level of the claim. A step remission rate is a description of a cohort's experience; a comparative claim needs a comparative design; a prediction for this patient needs her modifiers. Most disagreements about sequencing dissolve once the level is named.
depth.mistake:
The first error is assuming monotonic dose-response. It is intuitive, it is true for some drugs and some outcomes, and it is not true for the SSRIs at the doses used, which is why protocols built on it produce more side effects for no measured gain.

The second error is treating the four-to-six week threshold as a biological fact rather than a convention. It is a useful default, and it is not a boundary at which non-response can be declared with confidence; a person whose score is still falling at six weeks is on a trajectory, and the trajectory carries information a single cut-off discards.

The third error is reading the STAR*D step figures as a comparison of strategies. They are a description of an open-label sequence with attrition, preference-influenced choices and no placebo, and their most defensible content is the shape of the curve rather than the ranking of options.

The fourth error is forgetting that later steps enrol a selected group. The people who reach step three have already failed two treatments, so their lower remission rate is partly a statement about who they are. This is the same selection logic as lesson 81's prevalent pool, applied to a trial sequence.

The fifth error is the opposite of the first: concluding from the titration evidence that dose never matters. The average is close to zero and the interval is wide; individual patients differ, some drugs differ (venlafaxine is documented), and a considered trial of a higher dose in a particular person is compatible with the evidence provided it is monitored rather than assumed.

Diagnostic routine: ask whether the evidence concerns a dose, a policy, a cohort or a comparison, and answer at that level.
depth.application:
Choose one dose-response or titration paper and construct a three-column table, one row per dose or strategy.

Column one: the dose or policy, including the range if titration was flexible. Column two: the efficacy outcome with its definition and the number of participants contributing. Column three: the tolerability outcome (dropout for adverse effects, or the specific adverse event) with its rate.

Then annotate the table with three judgements. Whether the curve is rising, flat or falling for efficacy, and over what range. Whether the tolerability column moves in the same direction, and at what point the two columns cross. And which participants the row describes, since a trial that analysed completers describes a different population from one that analysed everyone randomised.

A worked miniature, using the titration review's own structure. Fixed minimum dose against placebo gives one effect estimate and one dropout rate; flexible titration above the minimum against placebo gives another. The ratio of odds ratios compares the two estimates, and for SSRIs it is 0.96 with an interval from 0.73 to 1.25: the table's message is a flat efficacy row and an unchanged tolerability row, which is the empirical basis for not treating escalation as the default next step.

Finally, write one sentence describing what a review at four weeks should measure, and one describing what would count as a reason to change strategy. If those two sentences cannot be written, the paper has not yet been converted into a decision.
depth.summary: Dose and duration are both non-linear in their effects. For SSRIs and mirtazapine, flexible titration above the minimum licensed dose has not added efficacy on average (ratio of odds ratios 0.96, 0.73 to 1.25), with venlafaxine the documented exception between 75 and 150 mg; the plateau has pharmacological and trial-mechanical causes. Response is distributed in time, so early improvement is a useful but imperfect predictor and a fixed week-four threshold misclassifies some eventual responders. STAR*D's step remission figures (37, 31, 14 and 13 per cent, cumulative 67 per cent) describe a cohort's experience of an open-label sequence, not a ranking of strategies.
