readings.title: Furukawa, T. A. et al. (2019), 'Optimal dose of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, venlafaxine, and mirtazapine in major depression: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis', Lancet Psychiatry 6(7):601-609 (reprinted in Focus 18(2):211-219)
readings.note: Open access reprint. Read the methods for how fixed-dose trials were used to estimate the dose-response curve, and the results for the finding that the lower part of the licensed range gives the best balance of efficacy and tolerability. Read the discussion for the authors' own caveats about the number of trials at higher doses and the limits of extrapolating beyond the studied range. This is the primary source for the plateau argument in this lesson.

readings.title: Furukawa, T. A. et al. (2020), 'No benefit from flexible titration above minimum licensed dose in prescribing antidepressants for major depression: systematic review', Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica 141(5):401-409
readings.note: Read the abstract for the design (123 trials, 29,420 participants) and the ratio-of-odds-ratios results: SSRIs 0.96 (0.73 to 1.25), venlafaxine 1.24 (0.96 to 1.60) overall but 1.30 (1.02 to 1.65) for titration from 75 to 150 mg, mirtazapine 0.77 (0.33 to 1.78). This is the study that separates a strategy question from a dose question. Full text paywalled; the abstract carries the estimates.

readings.title: Rush, A. J. et al. (2006), 'Acute and longer-term outcomes in depressed outpatients requiring one or several treatment steps: a STAR*D report', American Journal of Psychiatry 163(11):1905-1917
readings.note: Read the abstract for the per-step remission rates (36.8, 30.6, 13.7 and 13.0 per cent), the cumulative 67 per cent, and the finding that people requiring more steps relapsed more often in follow-up. Note what the design was: open-label, measurement-based, no placebo arm, with attrition between steps. Use it as an example of how a widely quoted number can be accurate and still support far less than it is usually asked to support.

visual.title: Two curves and the decision point between them
visual.description: A sketch of efficacy and tolerability against dose, with the strategy question (stay, titrate, switch) placed where the curves cross.
steps: Horizontal axis: dose from below the licensed minimum through the licensed range to above it. Vertical axis: effect, with two lines, one for efficacy and one for adverse-effect burden, both drawn from trial data rather than from theory.

Efficacy line: rises steeply at low doses, then flattens across most of the licensed range. Label the plateau with the ratio of odds ratios 0.96 (0.73 to 1.25) for flexible titration above the minimum dose, and mark the venlafaxine exception with a separate short segment rising between 75 and 150 mg.

Adverse-effect line: rises steadily across the same range. Label it with the dropout-for-adverse-effects rate, and add the note that in an intention-to-treat analysis this line feeds back into the efficacy line by removing people from the analysed group.

Crossing region: shade the zone where the gap between the lines is widest, and label it 'best balance', not 'maximum effect'. Note that the shaded zone sits in the lower part of the licensed range for SSRIs.

Second panel, time: a curve of symptom score against weeks for three trajectories, early responder, gradual responder, and non-responder, with the conventional four-week review marked. Label the misclassification zone where a gradual responder is still falling at the review.

Decision box beneath both panels: three arrows, stay and monitor, deliberate increase with a review, switch or augment, each with the observation that would justify it. Mark the box 'revisable' and note that the average effect close to zero does not forbid an individual trial.

lessons.title: Across a life: age, cohort, period and the burden that accumulates
lessons.explanation:
Lessons 81 to 84 treated time as the interval over which a case persists or a treatment works. This lesson treats time as a property of the person and of the population: how old someone is, which generation they belong to, and what was happening when they were measured. These three are routinely confused, and the confusion has consequences for who gets services and what is expected of them.

Begin with onset. In the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, lifetime prevalence of any DSM-IV disorder was 46.4 per cent, with anxiety disorders at 28.8 per cent, mood disorders at 20.8 per cent and impulse-control disorders at 24.8 per cent. Median age of onset was 11 for anxiety disorders, 11 for impulse-control disorders, 20 for substance use disorders and 30 for mood disorders. Half of all lifetime cases had begun by age 14 and three quarters by age 24. The distribution is the argument: most of the lifetime burden of mental disorder begins before adulthood, which means that a service system organised around adult referral is structurally late.

The same survey reported higher lifetime prevalence in more recent cohorts, with fairly stable intercohort differences across the life course. That finding demonstrates the identification problem in miniature. A difference between age groups measured in one survey can arise from how people change as they age, from differences between the generations being compared, or from what was happening in the year of the survey. Without repeated measurement of the same cohorts, the three cannot be separated, and the fact that they cannot be separated is a formal property of the design rather than a limitation of the analysts.

The burden figures add a second layer. In the Global Burden of Disease 2019 analysis, disability-adjusted life years attributable to mental disorders rose from 80.8 million in 1990 to 125.3 million in 2019, and the share of global disability-adjusted life years rose from 3.1 to 4.9 per cent. Over the same period, age-standardised rates barely moved, from about 1581 to 1566 per 100,000. The rise in the absolute figure is therefore mostly population growth and ageing, plus the relative change in other causes, not an increase in age-specific risk. Years lived with disability accounted for essentially all of the burden, 125.3 million years or 14.6 per cent of the global total, because deaths are attributed to mental disorders only for anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa in that analysis. Mental disorders are, in the technical sense, disabling rather than fatal, and their burden is accumulated over decades of life lived with impairment.

Mortality tells a different and more disturbing story. A meta-review of systematic reviews covering over 1.7 million patients and more than a quarter of a million deaths found increased all-cause mortality in every disorder examined, with risks for some disorders comparable to or larger than heavy smoking, and reductions in life expectancy of 10 to 20 years. Substance use disorders and anorexia nervosa had the highest all-cause mortality ratios; borderline personality disorder, anorexia nervosa, depression and bipolar disorder had the highest suicide risks. The review also noted that the quality of the underlying reviews was typically low, which is a caveat about precision rather than about direction.

Put together, these findings describe a pattern that any clinician working with older adults will recognise. A cohort of people with severe mental illness reaching later life has already been filtered by excess mortality, so survivors are not a random sample of those who became ill. A clinic for older adults will contain people who are unusually resilient and people whose physical illness is severe, and its composition will mislead anyone who reads it as a picture of the disorder's natural history. Diagnostic overshadowing, the attribution of physical symptoms to the psychiatric condition, compounds the problem and is one mechanism by which the mortality gap persists.
lessons.example:
A fictional study traces 300 people who were first admitted with a diagnosis of schizophrenia in 1985, and re-examines the survivors thirty years later. Of the original 300, 148 have died, 22 cannot be traced and 130 are re-assessed. Their mean symptom scores are lower than at first admission, 44 per cent meet criteria for remission, and only 18 per cent are in supported accommodation. A commentary concludes that schizophrenia burns out with age.

Examine the denominators before accepting the conclusion. The 130 survivors are 43 per cent of the original cohort. The 148 deaths, against an expected number derived from age and sex specific population rates, imply a standardised mortality ratio well above two, which is consistent with the meta-review evidence of a life expectancy reduction of 10 to 20 years. If the people who died were those with the earliest onset, the most severe illness and the poorest social circumstances, and the general finding in this literature is that they are, then the survivors are a selected group: the ones whose illness was least lethal, who had the most support, and who survived long enough to be found by a study that required survival and traceability.

Now separate the three clocks. The re-assessed group was diagnosed under criteria in use in 1985, which differed from current criteria, so part of any apparent improvement could be a cohort difference in what the label meant. The measurement is being made in a period when community care has largely replaced long-stay provision, so the social outcomes reflect services as much as illness. And the age effect, whatever it is, is confounded with both, because the same people are thirty years older and were diagnosed in a different era.

The defensible conclusion is narrower and still interesting: among people who survived thirty years after a first admission, a substantial minority are in remission and few require supported accommodation, which is worth knowing for planning and for hope. It says nothing about the natural history of the disorder in the original 300, because the outcome of greatest interest, death, removed nearly half of them before the assessment. A study that began with the incident cohort and followed it with complete ascertainment of deaths would answer the question the commentary asked; this study cannot, and its authors did not claim it could.
lessons.question: A fictional editorial states that depression is becoming more common because clinic data show that 30 per cent of today's 20-year-olds report depressive symptoms against 12 per cent of today's 70-year-olds, and concludes that ageing protects against depression. What is the central methodological problem?
lessons.answer: A single cross-section confounds age, cohort and period effects: the comparison mixes how people change with age, differences between the generations, and the conditions of measurement, and it adds differential survival and differential willingness to report, so no conclusion about ageing follows.
lessons.distractor: The problem is that self-report is unreliable in older adults, so the comparison should be repeated with a clinician-rated instrument before any conclusion is drawn.
lessons.correction: Changing the instrument would not fix the design, and it would introduce a new difference between the groups. The identification problem is that three time-related quantities vary together: age, birth cohort and measurement period. The older group grew up when the diagnostic vocabulary, the acceptability of reporting distress and the service response were different, and the younger group is being measured in a period of high public discussion of mental health. On top of that, the older group is a survivor cohort, and people with severe recurrent depression are less likely to be present in it. Any of these could produce the pattern without any effect of ageing. What would support the editorial's claim is repeated measurement of the same people over time, or a cohort-sequential design comparing several generations at the same ages. Until then the finding is a description of the data source, which is a narrower but still useful statement.

depth.definitions:
Age effect: change associated with growing older within individuals. Cohort effect: a difference between generations, arising from the circumstances they grew up in. Period effect: a change affecting all ages at a particular time, such as a change in diagnostic practice, service availability or public discourse. Identification problem: the impossibility of separating age, cohort and period effects from a single cross-section. Age standardisation: adjusting rates to a common age structure so that populations can be compared. Disability-adjusted life year: a year of healthy life lost, the sum of years lived with disability and years of life lost. Years lived with disability: the non-fatal component, weighted by severity. Standardised mortality ratio: observed deaths divided by those expected from age and sex specific rates. Survivor (healthy worker) effect: the depletion of a group by earlier death or exit. Diagnostic overshadowing: attributing physical symptoms to a psychiatric condition.

Prerequisite: lesson 81 on prevalence and duration, and lesson 43 on neurodevelopmental presentations across the lifespan.
depth.mechanism:
Why can age, cohort and period not be separated in one survey? Because each person contributes one number: their age at one moment. Age equals the survey year minus birth year, so the three quantities are linked by an identity, and any two determine the third. A statistical model that includes all three is therefore unidentifiable without an assumption, and the assumption smuggles in the answer. Repeated cross-sections allow period and age to be separated under constraints; following the same people allows age and cohort; nothing separates all three without a design feature that breaks the identity, such as a natural experiment in one period.

Why does the burden arithmetic behave as it does? Disability-adjusted life years sum years lived with disability and years of life lost. For conditions that cause little mortality, the second term is near zero and the total is essentially the first, weighted by severity. That is why mental disorders show large totals with almost no years of life lost, and why the totals track prevalence and duration rather than lethality. Age standardisation removes the effect of population age structure, which is why a rising total with a flat standardised rate is the signature of population growth and ageing.

Why does the mortality gap persist? Partly through direct mechanisms, including suicide, and substantially through physical illness: people with severe mental illness have higher rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease, receive poorer physical care, and present later. Diagnostic overshadowing is a named mechanism at the point of care, and systemic factors, including fragmented services and reduced access to screening, operate around it. The consequence for a clinician is that a cohort reaching later life is a selected sample, and the consequence for a service is that physical health monitoring is part of mental health care rather than adjacent to it.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting case where the period effect dominates and the cohort explanation is a distraction. A fictional children's service reports that referrals for eating disorders doubled between 2019 and 2022, and the local press attributes the rise to social media.

Three explanations are available and the data do not separate them. A period effect would be a change affecting all ages at once, such as a change in referral thresholds, waiting list publicity, or the pandemic's disruption of routines. A cohort effect would be a difference in the generation reaching adolescence, which social media use could plausibly cause, but which would accumulate gradually rather than doubling in three years. An ascertainment effect would be a change in who is counted, for instance a new pathway that captures people previously managed in primary care.

The informative check is disaggregation. If referrals doubled but the number of assessed cases with a confirmed diagnosis rose much less, ascertainment and threshold are doing the work. If the rise is concentrated in one age band and one presentation, a period effect specific to that group is more likely. If the rise persists in every subsequent cohort at the same age, a cohort explanation gains support. Each of these checks uses a comparison that the aggregate figure conceals, which is the practical response to an identification problem: find a comparison that varies one thing at a time.

The lesson is not that the press is wrong. It is that a doubling in referrals is compatible with at least three mechanisms, and that stating which mechanism is being claimed is the first act of appraisal. The same discipline applies to claims about rising rates in any service, and it is what separates a description of a pathway from a claim about the world.
depth.mistake:
The first error is reading a cross-sectional age difference as an ageing effect. It is the most common error in this area and the most consequential, because it shapes beliefs about what older people are like and what they need.

The second is ignoring survivor bias in older clinical samples. Because mortality is elevated across mental disorders, with life expectancy reductions of 10 to 20 years, the older patients a service sees are a selected group, and generalising from them to the disorder's course inverts the selection.

The third is treating disability-adjusted life years as a measure of service need. The metric weights severity and duration, not treatability, and a condition with a high burden may have no effective intervention available. Burden justifies attention; it does not specify what to do.

The fourth is reading a rising total as a rising risk. The GBD figures show totals rising by more than 50 per cent while age-standardised rates were essentially flat, and the difference between those two statements is the whole of population ageing.

The fifth is the inverse: dismissing burden figures because they are modelled. The estimates are produced by Bayesian meta-regression from prevalence, duration and severity inputs, and they carry uncertainty intervals and methodological choices; that makes them contestable in their details, not unusable in their shape.

Diagnostic routine: for any age-related claim, name which of age, cohort, period or selection could produce it, then ask what comparison would distinguish them.
depth.application:
Take one figure about mental disorder in a population, from a survey, a burden study or a service dataset, and write a 200 word decomposition.

First, identify the metric precisely: prevalence, incidence, disability-adjusted life years, years lived with disability, standardised mortality ratio, or service contact rate. State what its numerator and denominator are.

Second, state what would change it without any change in underlying risk: population growth, ageing, a change in diagnostic criteria or coding, a change in referral threshold, a change in survival.

Third, name the comparison the source uses, and whether it is age-standardised or crude. If the claim is about change over time, say whether the same people were followed or different people were sampled.

Fourth, write the strongest claim the figure supports and the strongest claim it does not.

A worked miniature. 'Mental disorders account for 4.9 per cent of global disability-adjusted life years, up from 3.1 per cent in 1990; age-standardised rates were stable at about 1566 per 100,000.' The supported claim: the absolute and proportional burden has grown with population size and age structure, and mental disorders are a large share of non-fatal burden. The unsupported claim: that people are becoming mentally ill at a higher rate. The distinction takes one sentence and prevents a decade of misdirected argument.
depth.summary: Most mental disorder begins young, with half of lifetime cases present by 14 and three quarters by 24, which makes adult-referred systems structurally late. A single cross-section cannot separate age, cohort and period effects, and older clinical samples are additionally selected by excess mortality. Burden figures show large and rising totals with stable age-standardised rates, which is the arithmetic of population ageing rather than of rising risk, and the mortality gap of 10 to 20 years is the reason late-life samples mislead. For any age-related claim, name the mechanism and the comparison that would distinguish it.

readings.title: GBD 2019 Mental Disorders Collaborators (2022), 'Global, regional, and national burden of 12 mental disorders in 204 countries and territories, 1990-2019', Lancet Psychiatry 9(2):137-150
readings.note: Open access. Read the findings for the totals used here (disability-adjusted life years from 80.8 million to 125.3 million; share of global total from 3.1 to 4.9 per cent; age-standardised rates 1581.2 against 1566.2 per 100,000; 125.3 million years lived with disability, 14.6 per cent of the global total). Read the methods to see how much of the estimate is modelled, and the limitations section for the authors' own statement of what the metric cannot support.

readings.title: Chesney, E., Goodwin, G. M. and Fazel, S. (2014), 'Risks of all-cause and suicide mortality in mental disorders: a meta-review', World Psychiatry 13(2):153-160
readings.note: Open access. Read the results for the range of standardised mortality ratios across disorders and the statement that several disorders carry mortality risks comparable to or greater than heavy smoking, with life expectancy reductions of 10 to 20 years. Read the section on the quality of the included reviews: the authors are explicit that most were of low quality, which bounds the precision of the estimates rather than their direction. This is the source for the survivor-selection argument.

readings.title: World Health Organization (2022), 'World mental health report: transforming mental health for all'
readings.note: Read the chapter on determinants and the life course for the argument that risk accumulates across development and that services organised around adult presentation miss the period of onset. Use it for the framing rather than for numbers, which are better taken from the primary sources above. The report is a synthesis and advocacy document, so its claims are pitched at the level of policy.

visual.title: Three clocks running at once, and the sample that only one of them produces
visual.description: A timeline diagram separating age, cohort and period, with the selection funnel that determines who appears in an older-adult clinic.
steps: Three parallel horizontal timelines: age (0 to 90), cohort (birth years labelled by generation), and period (calendar years with markers for diagnostic revisions, service changes and public events). Show the identity linking them: age equals period minus cohort.

Mark on the age line the onset distribution: half of lifetime cases by 14, three quarters by 24, with median onsets for anxiety (11), substance use (20) and mood (30). Annotate the implication for service design: adult referral is a late gate.

On the period line, mark a diagnostic revision and a change in referral threshold, with arrows fanning to all age bands to show a period effect. On the cohort line, mark a generational difference with arrows staying within one band to show a cohort effect.

Selection funnel from the population into an older-adult clinic: excess mortality removes a share of cases before age 65 (label 10 to 20 years of life expectancy reduction), leaving a survivor cohort. Add a second filter for help-seeking and a third for referral.
Resulting box, the late-life caseload: labelled 'selected by survival and referral', with a warning that its composition is not the natural history of the disorder.

Side panel, the burden arithmetic: a bar split into years lived with disability and years of life lost, with mental disorders showing almost all of the former, and a note that age standardisation is what separates a rising total from a rising rate.

questions.prompt: A fictional community mental health team reports that 34% of its current caseload meets criteria for a psychotic disorder, against a pooled community incidence of about 27 per 100,000 person-years. A manager concludes that the local area has an epidemic. Using lesson 81, what is the most important correction?
questions.answer: A clinic caseload is a prevalent pool, not a population: it accumulates people whose illness is long, who remain in contact, and who were referred, so a high proportion in the clinic is compatible with ordinary incidence and long duration. The comparable quantity is incidence in a defined population, not caseload composition.
questions.distractor: The manager is right to be concerned, because a caseload proportion that high can only arise from an incidence rate several hundred times the pooled estimate, and the team should audit its diagnostic practice before anything else.
questions.correction: The arithmetic of the clinic is the arithmetic of duration. Prevalence in a service is driven by incidence multiplied by how long people stay, and the clinic's denominator has already been filtered twice: by referral (who is sent) and by persistence (who stays). A team that sees mainly people with long illnesses will always over-represent them, whatever the local incidence. The managerial error is a denominator swap, treating a property of the caseload as a property of the population. The check lesson 81 supplies is to ask what the denominator is, what the sampling frame excluded, and whether the comparison quantity was measured on the same population and with the same ascertainment. Note also that incidence estimates themselves vary by case ascertainment: population registers report higher rates than first-contact designs.

questions.prompt: A fictional trust proposes to screen all new prisoners with a 12-item instrument for suicide risk. Validation in the development sample gives sensitivity 0.70 and specificity 0.75; the annual incidence of the outcome in this population is about 2%. An executive asks what proportion of those flagged will actually go on to the outcome.
questions.answer: Roughly 5 to 6 per cent. With a 2% base rate, of 1,000 people about 20 have the outcome and 14 of those are flagged (sensitivity 0.70), while about 245 of the 980 without it are also flagged (specificity 0.75), giving about 259 flags and a positive predictive value near 5.4%.
questions.distractor: About 70 per cent, because sensitivity is the proportion of true cases the instrument detects, so seven in ten flagged people will be true cases.
questions.correction: Sensitivity runs from cases to test, not from test to cases, and the two directions diverge as the outcome becomes rarer. At a 2% base rate even a fairly specific instrument generates many more false positives than true ones, so the flag identifies a group with modestly elevated risk rather than a group of future cases. This is why NICE guidance on self-harm advises against using risk scales to predict repetition, and why lesson 82 treats discrimination, calibration and predictive value as separate quantities. It is also why a screening programme's value lies in what happens after the flag (assessment, care, means safety), not in the accuracy of the flag itself.

questions.prompt: A fictional trainee summarises a maintenance trial: relapse 27% on continued antipsychotic against 64% on placebo over one year, and tells a patient that continuing treatment will cut her risk of relapse by about 60%. The patient asks what that means for her.
questions.answer: The relative reduction is real but is not her personal probability; the absolute difference is 37 percentage points over one year, so about three people must be treated for one year to prevent one relapse, and the same trial reports harms (weight gain 10% versus 6%, movement disorders 16% versus 9%) that belong in the same conversation.
questions.distractor: The figure of 60% is the correct way to express it, because risk ratios are the standard currency of trial reporting and converting to absolute terms would overstate certainty.
questions.correction: A risk ratio of 0.40 is arithmetically correct and communicatively misleading, because the same relative reduction means very different things at different baseline risks and because '60% less likely' invites a reading of 60% absolute protection. The patient-facing form is the pair of risks with their time frame plus the number needed to treat, and the harms, and the fact that the trial enrolled people who had already stabilised on treatment, which is a selected and adherent group. Lesson 83's discipline is to convert every relative statement into absolute terms, attach the time horizon, and ask who was in the trial before the number is used in a decision.

questions.prompt: A fictional clinic protocol states that patients who have not responded at the minimum licensed dose should have the dose doubled before any switch is considered, on the grounds that higher doses work better. A trainee asks what the dose-response evidence supports.
questions.answer: For SSRIs and mirtazapine, flexible titration above the minimum licensed dose has not been shown to add efficacy, tolerability or acceptability, and fixed-dose dose-response analyses place the best balance of efficacy and dropout at the lower part of the licensed range; the exception in that literature is venlafaxine between 75 and 150 mg.
questions.distractor: Dose-response is monotonic for all antidepressants, so doubling the dose is the evidence-based next step and switching should be reserved for people who fail two adequate trials.
questions.correction: The intuition that more drug means more effect is a hypothesis that the trials tested and largely failed to support. In a systematic review of 123 placebo-controlled trials with 29,420 participants, flexible titration above the minimum licensed dose gave a ratio of odds ratios of 0.96 (0.73 to 1.25) for SSRIs, with no important difference in tolerability, and only venlafaxine showed an advantage for titration to 150 mg. Note what this does and does not say: it is a statement about average effects in trial populations, not a prohibition for an individual, and dose changes are clinical decisions. The appraisal point is that an untested practice can be institutionalised in a protocol and then cited as if the protocol were evidence.

questions.prompt: A fictional commentary notes that clinic records show far lower rates of anxiety disorder among people over 70 than among people in their thirties, and concludes that anxiety burns out with age. Using lesson 85, what is the strongest objection?
questions.answer: A cross-sectional age difference cannot be assigned to ageing: it confounds age, cohort and period effects, and clinic records add selection, since older people who attend may differ from their birth cohort and those with long-standing difficulties may have left services or died.
questions.distractor: The finding is sound because the sample is large, and the only real limitation is that older people under-report symptoms, which would if anything make the true age decline steeper.
questions.correction: Three quantities are tangled in any single-year snapshot: how people change as they age, how cohorts differ because they grew up in different periods and were exposed to different diagnostic practice, and what happened in the year of measurement. They are not separable from one cross-section, which is why the identification problem is a formal one rather than a quibble. Add clinical selection and the direction of the bias becomes unpredictable: survivorship removes the most affected, help-seeking changes, and the diagnostic vocabulary of the cohort differs. The disciplined claim is narrower: in this data source, at this time, recorded anxiety is less common in the older group. What that implies about ageing is a separate question requiring longitudinal or cohort-sequential data.

units.title: From trial to service: pragmatic fit, monitoring, fidelity and scale

lessons.title: Pragmatic or explanatory: the trial that answers the question you are asking
lessons.explanation:
Lesson 78 established that a treatment effect is a difference, and that the control condition and the individual clinician are parts of what is being compared. This lesson adds the third part of the context: the conditions under which the trial was run. Two trials of the same therapy can produce very different estimates without either being wrong, because they answered different questions. The vocabulary for that difference is the explanatory to pragmatic continuum, and the instrument most often used to describe it is PRECIS-2.

An explanatory trial asks whether an intervention can work under favourable conditions. It restricts eligibility, uses expert delivery with close supervision, standardises the intervention, monitors adherence closely, and measures outcomes under controlled circumstances. Its priority is internal validity: the estimate should be attributable to the intervention rather than to confounders. A pragmatic trial asks whether an intervention does work under the conditions of ordinary practice. It recruits the people who would actually be offered the treatment, in ordinary settings, with the staff who would deliver it, allowing the flexibility that ordinary practice involves, and it measures outcomes that matter to participants and payers.

PRECIS-2 operationalises this across nine domains: eligibility criteria, recruitment, setting, organisation, flexibility in delivery, flexibility in adherence, follow-up, primary outcome, and primary analysis. Each is scored from 1 (very explanatory) to 5 (very pragmatic), producing a profile rather than a single number. The profile is the point. A trial can be pragmatic in its setting and explanatory in its eligibility, and the reader needs to see which. The instrument is explicitly not a quality rating: a score of 5 is not better than a score of 1, and its authors insist that the appropriate position on each domain depends on the question the trial was designed to answer.

The practical value appears when a service asks whether to adopt something. A trial that excluded people with comorbid substance use, delivered the therapy through doctoral-level staff with session recording and weekly supervision, and measured a symptom scale in completers has established efficacy under specified conditions. It has not established effectiveness in a service whose staff have different training, whose caseload includes the excluded groups, and whose patients stop attending. The gap is not a scandal; it is the ordinary consequence of a favourable test.

The size of that gap can be estimated rather than guessed. Consider the filters in sequence: eligibility removes the people least likely to respond, recruitment removes those who decline, delivery conditions raise the quality of what is provided, adherence monitoring raises the dose received, and follow-up conditions raise the completeness of measurement. Each filter pushes the estimate upward relative to routine practice. When a service imports the resulting number as a target, it imports the product of five favourable filters.

Complex interventions make the issue sharper because the intervention is a bundle. Collaborative care, for instance, combines a care manager, specialist supervision, a patient registry, and treatment adjustment guided by measurement. A Cochrane review of 79 randomised trials with 24,308 participants found consistent benefits for depression relative to usual care in the short term (standardised mean difference 0.34, 0.41 to 0.27), medium term (0.28) and long term (0.35), with benefits not demonstrated into the very long term. That evidence is comparatively pragmatic, because it was generated in real services, and it is still a statement about services that had the bundle. Remove the registry or the supervision and the entity being delivered is no longer the one that was tested, which is the subject of lesson 88.
lessons.example:
A fictional service lead is considering a 16-session psychological treatment for panic disorder and has two trials to read.

Trial A: 120 adults aged 18 to 65, no comorbid substance use or personality disorder, delivered by clinical psychologists with weekly supervision and session recordings, primary outcome a symptom scale at 16 weeks, analysed in completers. Effect size large. On PRECIS-2, eligibility scores 1 (highly restricted), organisation 1 (expert, closely supervised delivery), flexibility in delivery 2 (manualised), follow-up 2 (short and fixed), primary analysis 2 (completers). The profile is explanatory.

Trial B: 340 adults referred in ordinary practice, no exclusions beyond acute risk, delivered by psychological wellbeing practitioners with monthly supervision after training, primary outcome a patient-reported measure at 6 and 12 months, analysed by intention to treat with multiple imputation. Effect size moderate, about half of trial A's. On PRECIS-2, eligibility 4, setting 4, organisation 4, follow-up 4, analysis 5. The profile is pragmatic.

The service lead's question is which estimate applies to her clinic. Her patients resemble trial B's, her staff resemble trial B's, and her follow-up will resemble trial B's, so the pragmatic estimate is the more relevant starting point, even though it is smaller. Trial A remains useful for a different purpose: it establishes that the treatment has a specific effect that is not an artefact of poor delivery, which is what justifies training anyone in it at all.

What she should not do is average the two. They are estimates of different quantities in different populations, and a mean of them describes neither. What she can do is use trial B to plan capacity and expectations, and trial A to argue for the supervision that would move her service toward trial A's delivery conditions, with the honest acknowledgment that the move costs money and that the gain is an inference rather than a measured result.

Finally, she should check the comparator in both. If trial A compared the treatment with a waiting list and trial B compared it with usual care that included some psychological input, part of the difference between the two effect sizes is a difference in what they were measured against, which is lesson 78's point arriving in a new form.
lessons.question: A fictional commissioner rejects a pragmatic trial because 'it did not control confounding adequately and the therapists were not specialists', and prefers an explanatory trial with a larger effect. What is wrong with the reasoning?
lessons.answer: The commissioner has applied an internal-validity standard to a trial designed to answer an applicability question, then used the resulting preference to select the larger and less applicable estimate; the two trials answer different questions and the choice should follow the decision being made, not the size of the number.
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong: explanatory trials are higher in the evidence hierarchy precisely because they control confounding, so preferring them is the correct application of evidence-based practice.
lessons.correction: Evidence hierarchies rank designs for the question of whether an intervention can work, and they do not rank them for the question of whether it works here. A pragmatic trial that randomises in ordinary settings still controls confounding by randomisation; what it does not do is standardise delivery, and that is a feature, because the variability being tolerated is the variability the service will experience. Preferring the explanatory estimate because it is larger is a selection on result, which is the error lesson 77 described at the level of the literature and which operates equally at the level of a single decision. The defensible procedure is to specify the decision first, then choose the trial whose conditions match it, and to use the explanatory trial for the narrower claim it supports.

depth.definitions:
Efficacy: benefit under ideal, controlled conditions. Effectiveness: benefit under ordinary conditions of practice. Explanatory trial: designed to test whether an intervention can work, prioritising internal validity. Pragmatic trial: designed to test whether it does work in routine practice, prioritising applicability. PRECIS-2: a nine-domain instrument scoring trials from very explanatory (1) to very pragmatic (5) on eligibility, recruitment, setting, organisation, delivery flexibility, adherence flexibility, follow-up, primary outcome and primary analysis. Applicability: the degree to which trial conditions resemble the setting where the result will be used. Intention-to-treat analysis: analysis by randomised allocation regardless of what participants received. Contamination: delivery of the intervention to control participants, which dilutes a between-group difference. Cluster randomised trial: randomisation of groups rather than individuals, used where contamination is likely.

Prerequisite: lesson 78 on control conditions and therapist effects, and lesson 50 on reading a psychiatric study.
depth.mechanism:
Why do the two designs diverge systematically rather than randomly? Because each of the five filters between a population and an analysed trial sample moves in the same direction. Eligibility removes people with comorbidity and complexity, who respond less well on average. Recruitment removes people who decline or cannot attend, who are often the most disorganised or most sceptical. Delivery conditions raise the fidelity and skill of what is provided. Adherence monitoring raises the dose received. Measurement conditions, including short follow-up and complete data, remove the later relapses and the missing outcomes that would lower the average. Each is individually defensible and jointly produce an estimate that is an upper bound for routine conditions.

Why is the pragmatic trial not simply better? Because its estimate is less attributable. If routine practice varies in staffing, the difference between arms may reflect which staff happened to deliver which arm, and the trial may be underpowered for the smaller effect it is trying to detect. Pragmatic trials trade precision and causal clarity for applicability, and the trade is only worth making when the decision requires applicability.

Why does randomisation survive in a pragmatic design? Because randomisation addresses confounding by indication, which is the dominant threat in a clinical population, and it does so without requiring standardised delivery. What a pragmatic trial cannot fix is dilution: if control participants receive the intervention through ordinary channels, the contrast shrinks. That is why cluster and stepped-wedge designs are common in service research, and why those designs bring their own problems, including the need to account for clustering and the difficulty of blinding at the level of the cluster.

Why is a complex intervention's bundle indivisible? Because the effect estimate is attached to the whole configuration. A care manager without supervision, or a registry without a decision rule, is a different intervention with an unmeasured effect, and the trial's estimate cannot be transferred to it. This is why implementation fidelity, the subject of lesson 88, is a scientific issue rather than an administrative one.
depth.secondExample:
A contrasting design problem, where the pragmatic choice creates a measurement problem. A fictional region introduces a new model of crisis care and evaluates it with a stepped-wedge cluster trial: services are randomised to switch from the old model to the new one in a random sequence over eighteen months, and outcomes are compared within and between periods.

The design is appropriate because randomising individuals is impossible and because contamination within a service would be near total. It is pragmatic in setting, organisation and delivery. Its weaknesses are specific. Secular change is a threat, since the region is also implementing a waiting time target over the same period, so the wedge and the target move together. Outcomes are routinely collected, which makes them complete but dependent on coding practice, and coding practice changes when a new service is introduced because staff learn what to record. Blinding is impossible for staff, so the primary outcome should be one less susceptible to expectation, such as an administrative event rather than a clinician-rated scale.

The reading lesson is that pragmatism and rigour are not opposites, but they are in tension in specific places: the more a design resembles ordinary practice, the more the measurement inherits ordinary practice's artefacts. A well-reported pragmatic trial states which artefact it anticipated and what it did about it. A poorly reported one presents a routine outcome as if it were a research measurement, which is the same error as treating a validated scale as a measure of the construct without asking what it codes, as lesson 73 established.
depth.mistake:
The first error is treating PRECIS-2 as a quality score. It is a description, and a trial scoring 5 on every domain is not better than one scoring 1; it is answering a different question. The instrument's own authors are explicit that the appropriate position depends on the purpose.

The second error is assuming that efficacy implies effectiveness. The filters between a trial population and a clinic population are systematic, and the resulting gap is not a failure of the intervention but a predictable feature of the design.

The third is the reverse: dismissing explanatory trials as irrelevant to practice. They answer the question of whether there is a specific effect at all, which is what justifies the training, supervision and cost that pragmatic delivery requires. A service that only reads pragmatic trials will not know which components are worth protecting.

The fourth is treating a pragmatic trial as automatically applicable to a particular service. Pragmatic in the trial's setting does not mean pragmatic in yours; the relevant comparison is between the trial's organisation and your own, domain by domain.

The fifth is forgetting the comparator. A large effect against a waiting list and a small effect against active usual care may reflect the same underlying benefit; the difference is in the contrast, not in the treatment.

Diagnostic routine: before using an effect size, write the trial's profile on three domains that matter most for your decision, and state whether your service could reproduce them.
depth.application:
Take one randomised trial of a treatment you would plausibly deliver, and produce a PRECIS-2 profile with three annotations.

Score the nine domains from 1 to 5 using the definitions on the PRECIS-2 site, and record the evidence for each score in a phrase (for example, eligibility 1: 'excluded comorbid substance use and current suicidal ideation').

Then annotate. Annotation one: which three domains matter most for your setting, and why. Annotation two: whether your service could reproduce each of those three, and what it would cost. Annotation three: what the trial can and cannot say about your patients, stated in two sentences.

Finally, write the applicability statement in the form: 'This trial establishes that X can produce Y under conditions A, B and C. Whether it produces Y in this service depends on whether A, B and C can be reproduced, which would require ...'

A worked miniature. A trial of a brief intervention scores eligibility 2 (adults 18 to 65, no comorbidity), recruitment 3, setting 3, organisation 2 (research clinicians), delivery flexibility 2, adherence flexibility 3, follow-up 2 (12 weeks), outcome 3, analysis 3. The profile is mostly explanatory. The statement: the trial establishes that the intervention can produce a moderate reduction in symptoms when delivered by supervised research clinicians to a selected group over twelve weeks; whether that transfers to a service with a mixed caseload and monthly supervision is unknown, and the specific unknowns are the effect in comorbid patients and the effect under routine supervision.
depth.summary: Explanatory and pragmatic trials answer different questions, and PRECIS-2 profiles nine domains to show which question a trial answered. The gap between efficacy and effectiveness is produced by systematic filters, each of which raises the estimate relative to routine practice, and the gap is a feature of design rather than a scandal. Complex interventions are bundles, so an effect estimate belongs to a configuration that includes supervision, registries and decision rules. The choice between estimates should follow the decision being made, never the size of the number.

readings.title: Thorpe, K. E. et al. (2009), 'A pragmatic-explanatory continuum indicator summary (PRECIS): a tool to help trial designers', CMAJ 180(10):E47-E57
readings.note: Open access. Read the ten domains of the original instrument and the worked examples showing how the same intervention can sit at different points depending on design choices. This is the conceptual ancestor of PRECIS-2 and is clearer than the later tool about why each domain matters. Read the discussion of the instrument's limitations, including that scoring is a judgement.

readings.title: PRECIS-2 tool website, including the nine domain definitions and scoring guidance
readings.note: Use the domain definitions page for the nine domains and the 1 to 5 scoring anchors, and read the explicit statement that the tool is not a quality assessment and that there is no correct overall score. The site also hosts the worksheet, which is the practical instrument for the application task. This is a tool website rather than a peer-reviewed paper; cite the underlying publication when making an academic claim.

readings.title: Archer, J. et al. (2012), 'Collaborative care for depression and anxiety problems', Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 10:CD006525
readings.note: Read the results for the size and durability of effect (79 trials, 24,308 participants; short-term standardised mean difference 0.34, 0.41 to 0.27; medium-term 0.28; long-term 0.35; benefits not demonstrated into the very long term) and the description of what collaborative care consists of. The component list is the point for this lesson: the estimate belongs to the bundle. Note the heterogeneity in risk of bias across included trials.

visual.title: PRECIS-2 profile of two trials of the same therapy
visual.description: A radar-style sketch with nine axes, plotting an explanatory and a pragmatic trial, and a side panel translating the profile into an applicability statement.
steps: Nine axes arranged clockwise: eligibility, recruitment, setting, organisation, delivery flexibility, adherence flexibility, follow-up, primary outcome, primary analysis. Each axis runs from 1 at the centre (very explanatory) to 5 at the rim (very pragmatic).

Plot trial A as a small polygon close to the centre on eligibility, organisation, delivery flexibility, follow-up and analysis, with a note that the effect size is large and measured against a waiting list.

Plot trial B as a larger polygon reaching the rim on eligibility, setting, organisation, follow-up and analysis, with a note that the effect size is roughly half of A's and measured against usual care.
Shade the region between the polygons and label it: the applicability gap, produced by five filters (eligibility, recruitment, delivery conditions, adherence, measurement).
Side panel: the applicability statement in three lines, what the trial establishes, what it does not, and what the service would need to reproduce.
Footer note: the profile is not a score. A polygon covering the whole area is not a better trial than a small one; it is a different question.

lessons.title: Routine outcome monitoring: measuring, feeding back, and the difference between them
lessons.explanation:
Lesson 73 separated the properties a scale can have: consistency, structure, invariance across groups, and interpretability in terms of change that matters. This lesson adds the step that turns a scale into an intervention. The distinction it teaches is small in words and large in consequence: measuring a patient's progress and feeding that measurement back to the clinician in time to change the plan are different acts, and only the second has been shown to improve outcomes.

Three activities are routinely confused. Screening is a one-time application to identify people who may have a condition. Monitoring is repeated measurement to describe a trajectory. Measurement-based care is repeated measurement used to drive decisions at the level of the individual patient, which requires a score, a threshold, a rule for what to do when the threshold is crossed, and feedback delivered while the clinician can still act. The review that named the concept examined 51 articles and concluded that virtually all randomised trials with frequent and timely feedback of patient-reported symptoms to the provider during medication management or psychotherapy significantly improved outcomes, while one-time screening, infrequent assessment, and feedback to providers outside the clinical encounter were ineffective.

The effect sizes are modest, and where they concentrate is the interesting part. A meta-analysis of 24 studies of routine outcome monitoring found that two-thirds reported better outcomes than treatment as usual by the same practitioners, with mean standardised effects in the small to moderate range. The benefits were concentrated in patients predicted to have a poor outcome: feedback reduced deterioration rates and nearly doubled rates of clinically significant or reliable change in that group. Read that twice, because it describes a targeting mechanism rather than a general enhancement. Feedback helps most when it contradicts the clinician's expectation, which is when the patient is not improving as expected. For patients on track, a score that confirms the clinician's impression adds little.

The design of the evidence has features that limit how far it travels. Many studies are cluster randomised at the level of the clinician or the clinic, which is appropriate because the intervention is a change in practice, but which means the effective sample size is the number of clusters rather than the number of patients. Blinding is impossible: clinicians know whether they are receiving feedback. Novelty and attention are plausible contributors in short trials, and the same non-specific factors that lesson 78 described for psychotherapy apply to a feedback system introduced with enthusiasm and training.

Missing data are the quiet problem. A service in which the most unwell patients are least likely to complete measures will produce an outcome dataset that improves when nothing has changed, because the people whose scores would be high are absent. Lesson 73's point about instrument behaviour returns here at the level of the dataset: the measure's properties are the same, and the population contributing to the mean has changed.

Finally, the same numbers are used for at least three incompatible purposes: clinical decisions about an individual, supervision and professional development, and accountability or commissioning. A measure used for accountability creates incentives: to select patients, to record leniently, to choose a measure that moves. A measure used for clinical feedback aligns the incentive with the patient, because the clinician wants an accurate signal. Services that use one instrument for both purposes should expect the clinical signal to degrade, and the mechanism is not moral weakness but the ordinary response to being measured on a target.
lessons.example:
A fictional improving access to psychological therapies service introduces session-by-session symptom measures. In the first year, completion is 78 per cent and the mean score falls by 8 points across treatment. The service reports success. A new clinical lead asks three questions and finds that none can be answered.

Question one: for whom did the score fall? The mean conceals the distribution, and the distribution is what matters, because the intervention's mechanism is detecting people who are not improving. When the lead disaggregates, 31 per cent of patients improved by more than the reliable change threshold, 22 per cent were unchanged, and 9 per cent deteriorated, with 38 per cent missing at the final time point. The mean fall of 8 points is compatible with a service that helps many people slightly and misses the group the feedback was meant to catch.

Question two: what happened when a score did not fall? Nothing in the record indicates that anyone noticed. The measure was entered after the session, visible in the record but not in the room, and no threshold, rule or review was attached to it. This is monitoring without feedback, and the evidence would predict no effect.

Question three: who is missing? Completion is 78 per cent overall but 54 per cent among patients who started above the clinical cut-off. The group most likely to deteriorate is the group least represented in the outcome data, which means the reported improvement is partly a selection artefact.

The redesign follows from the three answers. The score is administered at the start of the session, not after it. A simple rule is adopted: a rise of five points or more, or no reliable improvement by session six, triggers a structured review of the formulation and the plan. The review is recorded. Completion by baseline severity becomes the quality indicator rather than overall completion, because that is the number that determines whether the data can be trusted. And the lead separates the clinical use of the measure from the performance report, so that the number clinicians see is the one that helps them and not the one that judges them.
lessons.question: A fictional trust reports that its outcome monitoring programme 'has not improved outcomes' after two years, despite collecting symptom measures at every appointment. An audit shows that scores are complete for 88 per cent of appointments, that clinicians view them only when opening the record, and that no threshold or action is specified. What is the most defensible conclusion?
lessons.answer: The programme as implemented is monitoring rather than measurement-based care: the evidence supports frequent, timely feedback used within the encounter to change the plan, and a score filed in a record without a decision rule does not meet that description, so the null result describes the implementation rather than the instrument.
lessons.distractor: The result shows that routine outcome measurement does not work in ordinary services, since a large naturalistic implementation with high completion is stronger evidence than the small trials that preceded it.
lessons.correction: A naturalistic implementation with high completion is strong evidence about implementation, and it is weak evidence about the intervention, because what was implemented is not the intervention that was tested. The review of measurement-based care is specific about the ineffective variants: one-time screening, infrequent assessment, and feedback delivered outside the clinical encounter. Viewing a score when opening a record is feedback of a sort, but it arrives without a threshold, without a comparison to the expected trajectory, and without a defined response. The correct next step is not to abandon measurement but to specify the loop: what score triggers what action, who reviews it, and when. If a properly specified loop then fails, that is a finding worth reporting.

depth.definitions:
Routine outcome monitoring: repeated administration of a standard measure during treatment. Measurement-based care: measurement used to drive individual clinical decisions, requiring a threshold, a rule and timely feedback. Feedback-informed treatment: a specific variant in which predicted treatment response is fed back with an alert for patients off track. Reliable change: change larger than the measurement error of the instrument, so that it is unlikely to be noise. Deterioration: reliable worsening during treatment. Off-track case: a patient whose observed progress is below the expected trajectory. Cluster randomised trial: randomisation of clinicians or clinics, appropriate where the intervention changes practice. Case-mix adjustment: statistical adjustment for differences in patient characteristics when comparing services. Teaching to the test: improvement in a measured indicator without improvement in the underlying construct.

Prerequisite: lesson 73 on what a measurement scale claims, and lesson 76 on average effects and the person in front of you.
depth.mechanism:
Why does feedback work at all? Because clinical judgement about trajectory is imperfect in a specific and correctable way. Clinicians see patients at intervals, recall the last impression rather than the last score, and are susceptible to optimistic drift when a patient is pleasant or improving slowly. A plotted trajectory makes a missed expected response visible. The feedback also creates a conversational opening: showing a patient that the score has not moved invites a discussion that might not otherwise occur, which is why the mechanism is described as collaborative rather than as an alerting system.

Why is the effect concentrated in off-track patients? Because for patients who are improving, the score confirms what the clinician already believes and changes nothing. The intervention has purchase only where expectation and data diverge. This explains why the average effect across all patients is small even when the effect in the target group is substantial, and it implies that a service's overall mean is the wrong metric for judging the programme.

Why do cluster designs dominate? Because the intervention is a change in how a clinician works, and a clinician cannot be randomised per patient without contaminating their practice. Randomising at the clinician or clinic level means the unit of analysis must match the unit of randomisation, and the effective sample size is the number of clusters, which is why these trials are usually underpowered and why their confidence intervals are wide.

Why does accountability degrade the signal? Because the same number cannot serve two masters. A clinician whose score determines their appraisal has an interest in the score being high, and the available actions (selecting patients, recording leniently, choosing the measure that moves) are not dishonest in intent; they are the ordinary response to a target. The design solution is structural separation: the clinical dashboard is for the clinician, and the accountability report uses a different, audited source.
depth.secondExample:
A different use of the same data, chosen because it fails in the opposite direction. A fictional regional body publishes a league table of services ranked by their mean improvement on a single measure. Two services with identical clinical quality appear at opposite ends: one serves an area with high deprivation and a high proportion of patients with chronic difficulties, the other serves an affluent area with a high proportion of brief episodes.

The ranking is measuring case mix as much as care. Mean improvement depends on who starts treatment and at what severity, and severity at baseline is strongly related to the room for improvement; services seeing more severe and more chronic patients will show smaller mean change even if their care is better. Case-mix adjustment is possible and imperfect, and the choice of adjustment variables is itself contestable.

The second failure is behavioural. Services in the lower half have three available responses: improve care, select easier patients, or record in ways that raise scores. The first is the intended one, and the third and second are common and difficult to detect. A league table that does not audit selection and recording will therefore measure a mixture of care, case mix and gaming, and it will not tell the reader the proportions.

The constructive version of the same exercise is to publish the indicator with its case-mix adjustment, its completion rate, and its distribution rather than its mean, and to use it for support rather than ranking. That is the difference between a measurement system that informs and one that invites its own corruption: not the instrument, but what is done with it and who is judged by it.
depth.mistake:
The first error is believing that measurement improves care by itself. The evidence is specific that it does not, and the specific failures are known: infrequent assessment, feedback outside the encounter, no threshold, no rule.

The second is reading the average effect as if it applied to everyone. It is concentrated in patients who are off track, so a service that monitors well and never identifies an off-track patient has implemented the paperwork and not the intervention.

The third is ignoring differential missingness. When completion falls as severity rises, the outcome data improve for reasons that have nothing to do with care, and every subsequent analysis inherits the bias.

The fourth is using the clinical instrument for accountability. This is not a moral criticism of managers; it is a design error with a predictable consequence, because people respond to what they are measured on.

The fifth is selecting a measure for its convenience rather than its properties. A short scale that is not sensitive to change, or whose minimal important difference is unknown, will produce a busy dashboard that cannot tell a real improvement from noise, which is lesson 73's argument reaching the ward.

Diagnostic routine: ask what the threshold is, who sees the score before the session, what happens when it is crossed, and what proportion of the most severe patients are missing from the data.
depth.application:
Design a measurement-based care loop for a service you know, in one page with four boxes.

Box one, the measure and the schedule: which instrument, at which points, administered by whom and when relative to the session. State the minimal important difference and the reliable change threshold, taken from the instrument's literature rather than guessed.

Box two, the rule: the specific conditions that trigger review (for example, no reliable improvement by session six, a rise of five points or more, or a score above the clinical cut-off at discharge planning), and who conducts the review.

Box three, the action: what the review consists of, in concrete terms, such as re-examining the formulation, checking adherence and dose, considering a change of modality, and recording the decision and its rationale.

Box four, the audit: completion rate by baseline severity band, proportion of off-track patients who received a review, and the outcome distribution rather than the mean. Meet monthly on these three numbers only.

A worked miniature. Measure: a depression scale at every session and at discharge. Rule: no reliable improvement by session six, or any increase of five points, triggers a 20 minute review within the next two sessions. Action: formulation revisited, adherence and dose checked, alternatives discussed with the patient. Audit: completion by severity, review rate among triggered patients, and the proportion deteriorating. The page is unglamorous and it is the difference between a programme that has been implemented and one that has been purchased.
depth.summary: Screening, monitoring and measurement-based care are different activities, and only the last has consistent evidence of benefit. The mechanism is timely feedback that contradicts expectation, which is why effects concentrate in patients who are off track and why the overall mean is the wrong metric. Completion that falls with severity makes outcome data look better while the programme does less, and using the clinical measure for accountability predictably degrades it. A loop needs a threshold, a rule, an action and an audit, and the audit should be by severity band rather than overall.

readings.title: Fortney, J. C. et al. (2017), 'A tipping point for measurement-based care', Psychiatric Services 68(2):179-188
readings.note: Read the abstract for the definition of measurement-based care and the review's key distinction: virtually all randomised trials with frequent and timely feedback during the encounter improved outcomes, while one-time screening, infrequent assessment and feedback outside the encounter did not. Read the discussion of aggregation for supervision and quality improvement. Full text is paywalled; the abstract carries the distinctions used here.

readings.title: Lambert, M. J., Whipple, J. L. and Kleinstäuber, M. (2018), 'Collecting and delivering progress feedback: a meta-analysis of routine outcome monitoring', Psychotherapy 55(4):520-537
readings.note: Read the abstract for the design (24 studies) and the findings: two-thirds of studies found feedback-assisted therapy superior to treatment as usual by the same practitioners, effects small to moderate, deterioration reduced and rates of clinically significant change nearly doubled among patients predicted to have a poor outcome. The concentration of benefit in the predicted-poor-outcome group is the mechanism this lesson relies on.

readings.title: Gaynes, B. N. et al. (2008), 'Primary versus specialty care outcomes for depressed outpatients managed with measurement-based care: results from STAR*D', Journal of General Internal Medicine 23(5):551-560
readings.note: Open access. Read the results for the near-identical remission rates in primary and specialty settings under the same measurement-based protocol (26.6 against 28.0 per cent by clinician rating; 32.5 against 33.1 by self-report) and the authors' conclusion that identical care produces identical outcomes. This is the cleanest demonstration that the protocol, not the setting, carries the effect, and it connects this lesson to lesson 86.

visual.title: The feedback loop, and the four places it breaks
visual.description: A circular diagram of the measurement-based care loop with break points marked, plus a panel showing what each break looks like in routine data.
steps: Loop, stage 1: patient completes a measure before the session. Break point A marked beside it: administered after the session, or completed at home and never returned, so the score cannot inform the encounter.

Loop, stage 2: score plotted against the expected trajectory, with the reliable change threshold drawn as a band. Break point B: score displayed as a single number with no trajectory and no threshold, so the clinician cannot see whether it has moved meaningfully.
Loop, stage 3: rule triggers a structured review for off-track patients. Break point C: no rule exists, so nothing happens when the score fails to improve, which is monitoring rather than care.

Loop, stage 4: review changes the plan and the change is recorded. Break point D: review happens informally and is not recorded, so the service cannot tell whether the loop operated or whether outcomes changed.
Side panel, the audit: three numbers only, completion by baseline severity band, proportion of triggered patients who received a review, and the outcome distribution rather than the mean.
Footer: the separation rule, clinical dashboard for the clinician, audited and case-mix adjusted indicator for accountability, with a note that combining them degrades the clinical signal.

lessons.title: Fidelity, adaptation and drift: what happens to a programme in its second year
lessons.explanation:
Lesson 86 established that an effect estimate belongs to a configuration of conditions, and lesson 79 established that services are systems in which a new activity displaces an old one. This lesson is about the interval between the trial and the second year of routine delivery, where most of the loss occurs. It introduces the vocabulary that lets a service describe what it is actually delivering, and it separates two things that are usually merged: planned adaptation, which is a design decision, and drift, which is an accumulation of small abandonments.

The first move is to separate implementation outcomes from clinical ones. The standard taxonomy names eight: acceptability (whether the intended users find it agreeable), adoption (the intention or action to employ it), appropriateness (perceived fit), cost, feasibility, fidelity (the degree to which it was delivered as designed), penetration (how far it reached the eligible population) and sustainability (whether it is maintained). These are outcomes in their own right, and they are the ones that determine whether a clinical outcome can be attributed to the programme at all. A service that reports a clinical result without reporting penetration and fidelity cannot say what produced it.

Fidelity itself is not one thing. The dimensions usually distinguished are adherence (whether the prescribed components were delivered), dose or exposure (how much was delivered, and how much was received), quality of delivery (how well), participant responsiveness (how engaged people were), and programme differentiation (how distinct the programme is from what would have happened anyway). A programme can score well on attendance and poorly on adherence, which is why attendance figures are a weak fidelity measure and why the honest version requires observation or structured self-report against explicit criteria.

The empirical case for caring is strong in aggregate. A review of more than 500 studies of promotion and prevention programmes concluded that the level of implementation affects the outcomes obtained, and identified at least 23 contextual factors influencing implementation, spanning the community, providers, the innovation itself, organisational functioning and the support system of training and technical assistance. That review is about prevention programmes rather than psychiatric treatment, which is a limit on its transfer, but the direction of the finding is consistent with the treatment literature: what is delivered is not what was designed, and the difference is measurable.

The harder question is what should be held fixed. The useful distinction is between core functions and peripheral forms. Core functions are the mechanisms believed to produce the effect, such as the presence of a care manager, a measurement-based decision rule, or a supervised caseload. Peripheral forms are the surface features, such as session length, the language of the manual, or the mode of delivery. Adaptation that preserves function and alters form is usually appropriate, and often necessary for cultural fit; adaptation that silently removes function is drift, regardless of how reasonable each individual change seemed.

Sustainment is the final stage and the least studied. A review of the sustainability literature found that definitions vary widely, that the evidence base is thin, and that many programmes are not maintained once external support ends. The reasons are structural rather than motivational: staff turn over, funding cycles end, the champion moves, and the programme's activities are absorbed into general duties without their supervision. The practical implication is that sustainment has to be designed at the outset, with named owners, protected time, and a measure that survives the departure of the person who started it.
lessons.example:
A fictional early intervention in psychosis service is rolled out from a single well-resourced site to ten sites in a region. The original site had a caseload cap of 15 per care coordinator, weekly individual supervision, a family intervention component of at least six sessions, and a physical health check within six weeks. Twelve months after rollout, an evaluation finds that the pooled readmission reduction has fallen from the pilot's 40 per cent to 18 per cent.

Break the programme into its functions and measure each. Caseload: six of ten sites are at or above 25. Supervision: four sites hold weekly supervision, three hold monthly, three hold it irregularly. Family intervention: recorded for 34 per cent of families against 81 per cent at the pilot site, with a median of two sessions rather than six. Physical health check: 47 per cent within six weeks, against 92 per cent at the pilot.

Now the reading. The pilot estimate was produced by a configuration with low caseloads, weekly supervision and a family component delivered at dose. The new sites are delivering a recognisably different intervention: the case management is present, the family work is largely absent, and the supervision that would have detected the drift is itself reduced. Pooling across sites mixes implementations, and the pooled figure describes an average of things that differ.

The evaluative error to avoid is the inference that the model does not work at scale. What the data support is narrower and more useful: the model as configured at the pilot site cannot be delivered at ten sites with this staffing, and the specific constraints are caseload and supervision capacity. That is a finding about the region's workforce, and it is actionable in a way that a verdict about the model is not.

The response has three parts. Define the non-negotiable functions explicitly, with thresholds: caseload at or below 20, weekly supervision, family intervention offered to every family with at least four sessions attended, physical health check within eight weeks. Report fidelity against those four every quarter, at site level and not only pooled. And where a site cannot meet the threshold, record the reason, because a fidelity failure caused by a vacancy is a different problem from one caused by a decision that the component was unnecessary.
lessons.question: A fictional team cannot recruit a family therapist, so it replaces the family intervention component with a single psychoeducation session for relatives. The team lead describes this as 'adapting the model to local capacity'. Using this lesson's terms, how should the change be classified and what should happen to the evaluation?
lessons.answer: It is drift rather than planned adaptation, because a core function (sustained family work) has been replaced by a peripheral form of contact; the site is delivering a different intervention, so its outcomes should be reported separately and the fidelity measure should record the substitution rather than averaging it away.
lessons.distractor: It is legitimate adaptation, since local capacity is a real constraint and the model's guidance encourages flexibility; no change to the evaluation is needed provided the single session is recorded.
lessons.correction: The distinction that matters is whether the change preserves the mechanism. Family intervention in early psychosis is a dosed, skills-based component whose effect depends on multiple sessions with the family system; a single psychoeducation session is a different and much smaller intervention. Calling that adaptation uses the vocabulary of flexibility to describe a reduction in dose, and the consequence is that the site's results are attributed to a model it is not delivering. The honest handling is to record the deviation as a protocol variation, analyse the site separately or with fidelity as a covariate, and treat the gap as a workforce finding to be solved rather than as evidence about the model.
